info.bio:
David Robert Jones (8 de enero de 1947 - 10 de enero de 2016), más conocido como David Bowie, fue un cantante polifacético, inclasificable dentro de un solo género, ya que su música involucra diversos estilos musicales como el rock, el pop y la música electrónica. Fue también compositor, multiinstrumentista, productor, artista plástico y actor británico, fuertemente influyente en varias generaciones. Fue un ícono de la música y uno de los músicos más influyentes de la música contemporánea.

Nació en Brixton, un área de Londres, pero creció en el pueblo de Bromley, en Kent (actualmente parte del Gran Londres). Su carrera de músico comenzó en la década de los 60 como saxofonista y vocalista de varios grupos de blues, uno con los que pudo llegar a grabar fue The Manish Boys. Su nombre artístico fue obligado debido a la popularidad de Davy Jones, de The Monkees. El apellido Bowie fue elegido en honor del famoso personaje del Far West Jim Bowie. Desde 1992 estuvo casado con la modelo Iman, con la que tuvo a su hija Alexandria, aunque fue con Angela Barnett (Angie), su anterior mujer, con quien tuvo a su hijo Zowie, ahora conocido como Duncan Jones, reciente ganador del premio BAFTA a mejor director por su opera prima "Moon".

Una de las señas de identidad más carismáticas fue la diferencia de color de su ojo izquierdo, el cual fue dañado con un compás en una pelea en el colegio.

Es reconocido por su gran poder de cambio y adaptación (en algunos casos incluso anticipadamente) a las nuevas tendencias musicales, es por ello que es conocido por el sobrenombre de "Camaleón". . scenes.name: El verano de 1966
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Las listas preferían canciones de relajación y huida: «Hanky Panky», «Wild Thing», «Sunny» de Bobby Hebb, el «Summertime» de Billy Stewart, «Sunshine Superman» de Donovan y, sobre todo, «Summer in the City» de los Lovin’ Spoonful, número 1 en agosto, con taladros y bocinas en las pausas; su anuncio en Billboard (niños negros jugando con una boca de incendios) se cumplió con el motín de la boca de riego del West Side de Chicago. En Inglaterra, tras ganar el Mundial, sonaban «Out of Time» de Chris Farlowe (de Jagger y Richards, en Immediate) y «Sunny Afternoon» de los Kinks, el suspiro de un boom que se deshinchaba con la congelación de salarios de Wilson (20 de julio): fin de los altos sesenta británicos. Los Who acabaron a patadas el festival de jazz y blues de Windsor. John Rechy puso «Dirty Water», «Hungry», «Summer in the City» y «Paint It, Black» de banda sonora a la desesperación de Numbers.
scenes.family: Pop de estudio: Spector, Beach Boys, Meek

scenes.name: El fin del boom del beat británico
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Los Beatles habían empezado el ciclo a principios de 1963 y lo cerraron en septiembre de 1966. El ritmo implacable (tres singles al año, cientos de conciertos, fama mundial) pasó factura: crisis y hospitalizaciones (Jagger en junio, el aparente intento de suicidio de Scott Walker en agosto), Brian Jones desaparecido, Paul Jones dejó Manfred Mann, los Animals se rehicieron como New Animals, Georgie Fame disolvió los Blue Flames. La novela All Night Stand de Thom Keyes, un roman à clef sobre los Beatles, acaba con su estrella aburrida de sí misma. Sin el centro unificador de los Beatles volvió el entretenimiento ligero (los Bachelors, Ken Dodd y «Distant Drums» del difunto Jim Reeves, número 1 casi todo octubre), mientras en agosto la mitad del Top 50 británico era americana: Motown y los grupos de la Costa Oeste. «Una era ha terminado», escribió Chris Welch.

scenes.name: Glam arty: Bowie, Roxy Music y Eno
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: El costado intelectual del glam. Bowie, «el más grande diletante del rock», fue la inspiración clave del ethos postpunk del cambio constante; Roxy Music y los discos solistas proto-new wave de Brian Eno, con sus ruidos de sintetizador, anticipan el sonido de la década siguiente.
scenes.family: Antecedentes: punk, art rock, kraut y glam

scenes.name: Bowie e Iggy en Berlín
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Más que Never Mind the Bollocks o el debut de The Clash, al postpunk lo marcaron los cuatro discos de Bowie de 1977: Low y Heroes, y The Idiot y Lust for Life de Iggy Pop. Grabados en Berlín, se alejan de Estados Unidos y del rock'n'roll hacia un sonido europeo, frío y controlado, sobre los ritmos motorik de Kraftwerk y Neu!, con los sintetizadores al mismo nivel que las guitarras. El lado dos de Low, con Brian Eno («texturólogo supremo»), es una suite de atmósferas crepusculares. Eno se convierte después en uno de los productores que definen la era (no wave, Devo, Talking Heads, U2).
scenes.family: Antecedentes: punk, art rock, kraut y glam

scenes.name: New romantics y la escena del Blitz
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: En el club Billy's y luego el Blitz, Rusty Egan pincha Bowie de Berlín, Iggy, Moroder, Kraftwerk, «Being Boiled», Telex y Yellow Magic Orchestra, y Steve Strange guarda la puerta: maquillaje, sombreros españoles y cortes geométricos, fantasía y escapismo tras ocho horas de trabajo. Visage, superbanda de punks fracasados (Ure, Currie, tres de Magazine), con la tristeza sobrenatural de «Fade to Grey»; Spandau Ballet, elitista y nietzscheano antes de volverse soul; Ultravox reformado con Midge Ure y la glacial «Vienna» (1981). Bowie lo corona con «Ashes to Ashes», con Strange vestido de Pierrot. Martin Rushent, con su sello Genetic, llegó a tenerlos a casi todos.

scenes.name: Segunda invasión británica y MTV
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: En 1982 el new pop deja de ser un sueño de periodistas: «Don't You Want Me», «Tainted Love» y «The Look of Love» anuncian una nueva invasión, y en 1983 la segunda camada (Duran Duran, Culture Club, Wham!, Eurythmics, Thompson Twins) conquista Estados Unidos gracias a MTV, canal ideado por Michael Nesmith que, sin vídeos americanos, dependía de los británicos, más videogénicos y cultivados en el estilo («I want my MTV»). A Flock of Seagulls, Altered Images («Happy Birthday»), Simple Minds («Promised You a Miracle», New Gold Dream), Haircut 100, Kajagoogoo; Bowie se broncea con «Let's Dance». El new pop reexporta música negra (Chic, P-Funk, Quincy Jones) a la América blanca. En el Reino Unido, 1983 se vive en cambio como un año infausto: reelección de Thatcher, «Kill Ugly Pop» en las paredes y la vuelta de la conciencia social.

scenes.name: Decadencia y glam-rock
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: El rock siempre tuvo un elemento de decadencia, amoralidad y obscenidad; entre los Cockettes (1968) y el Rocky Horror Picture Show (1974) se convierte en producto de masas. Gran Bretaña lo llama glam-rock: T.Rex lo inaugura y lo casa con el hard rock; David Bowie lo lleva a su cima comercial convirtiendo el marketing en arte (Ziggy Stardust, la trilogía berlinesa con Eno). En EE UU, Alice Cooper, Sparks, Iggy Pop y Lou Reed (Berlin, Metal Machine Music, New York). El glam y la decadencia preparan el punk: Mott The Hoople, Be Bop Deluxe, New York Dolls, Heartbreakers, Dictators, Modern Lovers de Jonathan Richman, Runaways.
scenes.family: Punk, new wave, hardcore y noise

scenes.name: Tekno de Fráncfort: Talla 2XLC
scenes.book: Techno Rebels: The Renegades of Electronic Funk
scenes.author: Dan Sicko
scenes.desc: Tras el pico de la influencia de Kraftwerk en el rock (la trilogía berlinesa de Bowie), surgió en Fráncfort otro «techno» o «tekno», atribuido a Talla 2XLC (Andreas Tomalla), que dirigía el sello Zoth Ommog, fundó el «Technoclub» del Dorian Gray y la revista Frontpage, y estaba en Moskwa TV («Tekno Talk», 1985). A diferencia del de Detroit, venía del hi-NRG y el EBM, estilos europeos. A mediados de los noventa Detroit, Fráncfort y Berlín se mezclaban y la polémica sobre el origen de la palabra seguía viva.
scenes.family: Europa: rave británico, Bélgica, Berlín, Países Bajos

scenes.name: Art-rock
scenes.book: Loops 1 y 2. Una historia de la música electrónica
scenes.author: Javier Blánquez (ed.)
scenes.desc: La vanguardia del rock neoyorquino, influida por el pop-art, el minimalismo y el proto-punk, usa los sintetizadores para deformar su lenguaje.

scenes.name: Kraftwerk y el synth-pop pionero
scenes.book: Loops 1 y 2. Una historia de la música electrónica
scenes.author: Javier Blánquez (ed.)
scenes.desc: Kraftwerk tuvo la idea que llevaría la electrónica al gran público: usar la paleta del sintetizador para canciones pop pegadizas como «Autobahn».

scenes.name: Nuevos románticos
scenes.book: Loops 1 y 2. Una historia de la música electrónica
scenes.author: Javier Blánquez (ed.)
scenes.desc: Movimiento londinense que rescata del glam el maquillaje y la pose, con un uso coyuntural de la tecnología: Ultravox (con John Foxx primero), Japan, Visage de Steve Strange, Duran Duran, Spandau Ballet, ABC, la pose kraftwerkiana de Gary Numan y, después, Culture Club.

mentions.text: …opened the golden age of glam-rock, and Electric Warrior (1971) was the album that wed this genre to hard-rock, a crucial intuition. However, it was David Bowie (2) who brought glam-rock to its commercial (if not artistic) peak. While his musical skills are dubious at best, there is no question that Bowie performed a Copernican revolution, turning marketing into the essence of his art. All great phenomena (and swindles) of popular music, from Elvis Presley to the Beatles, had been, first and foremost, marketing phenomena, but Bowie transformed that marketing phenomenon into an art on its own. Bowie was, in many ways, the heir, no matter how perverted, of Andy Warhol's pop art and of the underground culture of the 1960s. He adopted some of the most blaspheme issues and turned them upside down to make them precisely what they had been designed to fight: a commodity. Bowie embodied the quintessence of artificial art, raising futulity to paradigm and focusing on exhibition rather than on content. Bowie made irrelevant the relevant and relevant the irrelevant. podcast.title: 1964 British Television and Newspaper Appearance for Long Hair Rights
podcast.body: In 1964, under his birth name David Jones, Bowie appeared on British television and in newspapers alongside other members of the International League for the Preservation of Animal Filaments to publicly defend the right of men to have long hair. "In 1964, Bowie, who was still known as David Jones at the time, appeared on British television and also in the newspapers with a few members of this association to defend the right of a man to have long hair."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 1964 TV Appearance - League for the Protection of Animal Filaments
podcast.body: On November 12th, 1964, at the age of 17, David Jones appeared on television as a spokesman for a fictitious group called the "League for the Protection of Animal Filaments." This was a scam designed to get his friends on TV and earn about five pounds each, ostensibly supporting men with long hair. "He appeared as a spokesman for the league for the protection of animal filaments, a totally fictitious support group for men who chose to wear their hair long."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: British TV Appearance for Long Hair (1964)
podcast.body: At just 17 years old in 1964, Bowie gained sporadic attention by appearing on British television to defend the right of men to have long hair. He acted as the spokesman for an organization humorously named the International League for the Preservation of Animal Filament. "He was the spokesman for an organization known as the International League for the Preservation of Animal Filament."

podcast.title: Early Activism for Long Hair (1964)
podcast.body: At the age of 17, David Bowie gained public attention in 1964 by appearing on British television and in major newspapers as the spokesman for the "International League for the Preservation of Animal Filament." This organization was essentially a support group for men who preferred to wear long hair, similar to women's hair.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early TV Appearance (November 12, 1964)
podcast.body: At 17 years old, David Jones appeared on television as a spokesman for "The League for the Protection of Animal Filenet." This was a completely fictitious support group created by him and his friends for men with long hair, designed as a scam to get on TV and earn about five pounds each. "In 1964, at the age of 17, he appeared as a spokesman for the league for the protection of animal filenet, a totally fictitious support group for men who chose to wear their hair long."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Name Change to Avoid Confusion (1966)
podcast.body: In 1966, David Jones changed his name to David Bowie to prevent being confused with Davey Jones, the "cute little English dude" from the popular TV show, The Monkees. "In 1966, David Jones would change his name to David Bowie to avoid being confused with Davey Jones, who was the cute little English dude on the TV show The Monkeys."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Career Experiments (1967-1969)
podcast.body: During this period, Bowie extensively experimented to find his artistic niche. His endeavors included living in a Buddhist monastery, taking dance lessons, learning to become a mime, working in a printing shop, and being cast in an ice cream commercial. The commercial was notably directed by a then-unknown Ridley Scott. "Between 1967 and 1969, Bowie tried to find his niche. He experimented with all kinds of different things."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Experiments and Mime Training (1967-1969)
podcast.body: Between 1967 and 1969, Bowie extensively experimented with various endeavors to find his niche. He lived in a Buddhist monastery, took dance lessons, learned mime, worked in a printing shop, and even appeared in an ice cream commercial directed by the then-unknown Ridley Scott. "He experimented with all kinds of different things."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Love Ice Cream Commercial (1969)
podcast.body: David Bowie appeared in a commercial for a brand of ice cream called Love in 1969. The commercial was directed by renowned filmmaker Ridley Scott. "In 1969, David Bowie appeared in a commercial for Ice Cream."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Concept of Selling Out: Part 1

podcast.title: "Man Dress" Controversy (November 1970 - June 1971)
podcast.body: David Bowie's decision to wear a full-length blue dress on the original cover of *The Man Who Sold the World* album in November 1970 was a highly controversial move in America. At the time, Bowie had little reputation in the US, and the country was not "ready for a feminized rocker." This led to record stores refusing to stock the album until RCA Records provided an alternative cover, and even an incident where a gun was pulled on Bowie in Texas. "America, not ready for a guy wearing a dress."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 1

podcast.title: Golden Period - 1970-1983
podcast.body: Bowie experienced an incredibly prolific and impactful "golden period" from 1970 to 1983, during which he released 13 albums, many of which became not only classics but milestones in rock history. "He had a golden period that stretched roughly from 1970 through to 1983, 13 albums in those 13 years, and many of them remained not just classics, but milestones in the history of rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Hype Costumes (1970)
podcast.body: In 1970, with his band Hype, Bowie began experimenting with stage costumes. They wore superhero outfits made from shiny material, thigh-high boots, and Bowie's own costume included a cape and the word "rainbow man" sewn on his chest, a stark contrast to the hippie fashion of the time. "In 1970, around the time Mark Bowen was gaining fame with Ride-A-White Swan, Bowie had a band called Hype. They began appearing in interesting costumes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

podcast.title: Interview in Jeremy Magazine (1970)
podcast.body: In January 1970, David Bowie became one of the first pop stars to be interviewed by Jeremy, a gay magazine. Although the article itself did not focus on his sexuality, the mere fact of his appearance in a gay publication was considered radical, especially given that just three years prior, being gay was still a jailable offense in the UK. "the very fact that he appeared in a game egg was pretty radical."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Early Days of LGBTQ Rock

podcast.title: Manager Tony DeFries' Early Guidance (1970-1972)
podcast.body: Tony DeFries, a solicitor by profession, signed on as Bowie's manager in 1970 when Bowie was a struggling young singer. Within approximately 18 months, DeFries secured Bowie a new deal with RCA records and proceeded to transform him into an international star. The entirety of Bowie's early 1970s career, including the iconic Ziggy Stardust era, was carefully guided by DeFries.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Limited US Reputation and Promotional Tour Challenges (1971)
podcast.body: In 1971, David Bowie was only "big-ish" in Britain and had "absolutely no reputation whatsoever" in the United States. Due to immigration and work permit issues, he was unable to officially tour for *The Man Who Sold the World*, instead conducting private concerts for journalists from his hotel room bed. "Bowie was only big-ish in Britain and had absolutely no reputation whatsoever in the United States."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 1

podcast.title: Meeting Iggy Pop (September 7, 1971)
podcast.body: David Bowie met Iggy Pop in New York on September 7, 1971, while Bowie was preparing for his Ziggy Stardust phase. This meeting marked the beginning of a significant partnership between the two artists. "The date was September 7th of 1971."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

podcast.title: "Coming Out" Statement and LGBTQ+ Impact (1972)
podcast.body: In January 1972, Bowie gave a "flippin' quote" to a British music paper, stating he had "always been gay." This statement, unthinkable for a celebrity at the time, given the legal context of homosexuality in Britain (decriminalized in England/Wales only in 1967, still illegal in Scotland/Northern Ireland for years, and military ban), became a bomb. Despite Bowie later recanting claims of being gay or bisexual, this declaration resonated with thousands who were afraid to come out, giving them courage. "This coming out struck a chord with thousands of people who wanted to do the same thing but were too afraid."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Contractual Dispute with Main Man (1972-1975)
podcast.body: David Bowie wanted out of his contract with Tony DeFries' management company, Main Man, by the end of 1974, just two years into their relationship. Despite selling millions of albums, Bowie realized that most of the profits were not reaching him, suspecting that the new contract signed with Main Man at the end of September 1972 was "weird." On January 29, 1975, Bowie informed RCA, his record label, of his intention to split from DeFries, sparking a battle over who owned Bowie's next album.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Debut of Ziggy Stardust (July 8, 1972)
podcast.body: On July 8, 1972, David Bowie introduced the world to his character Ziggy Stardust at the Royal Festival Hall in London. This marked the genesis of the "world's first synthetic, pre-packaged, ultra-theatrical rock star," lasting 360 days and becoming a highly influential piece of marketing and PR in rock history. "That night, David Bowie stepped on stage at the Royal Festival Hall in London and introduced himself by saying, hi, I'm Ziggy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 1

podcast.title: Flippant "Gay" Quote (January 1972)
podcast.body: In January 1972, Bowie gave a flippant quote to a British music paper stating he had "always been gay." This statement was an enormous "bomb" at the time, given that homosexuality had only been decriminalized in Britain for over-21s in England and Wales in 1967, and was still criminalized elsewhere in the UK. This public declaration, despite its flippant nature, profoundly resonated with thousands of gay and confused individuals. "In January, 1972, Bowie gave a flippant quote to a British music paper about having always been gay."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Melody Maker Interview (January 1972)
podcast.body: In early 1972, Bowie gave a front-page interview to British music weekly Melody Maker, titled "Oh, You Pretty Thing." The article described his image as a "swishy queen, a gorgeously effeminate boy," noting his "camp" demeanor while he maintained he was "ungay." This interview showcased his deliberate push for shocking outrage and sexual ambiguity. "He gave an interview to Melody Maker, one of the big British music weeklies. The title of the article was, oh, you pretty thing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

podcast.title: NME Interview Coming Out (1972)
podcast.body: On January 22nd, 1972, Bowie gave an interview to the NME, a major British weekly music tabloid, where he famously stated, "I'm gay and I always have been." While later acknowledged as a publicity stunt, the impact of those seven words was immense and incalculable, giving hope to closeted individuals globally. "I'm gay and I always have been."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Early Days of LGBTQ Rock

podcast.title: Peele Session (May 23rd, 1972)
podcast.body: David Bowie, accompanied by his band The Spiders from Mars, recorded a session for DJ John Peel on May 23rd, 1972. These "Peele Sessions" were a notable part of BBC programming, allowing artists to record live off the floor to circumvent "Needle Time" restrictions. "Here's something from May 23rd, 1972, when an artist on the asset named David Bowie dropped in for a session with his band, The Spiders from Mars."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Music vs Technology Over The Years

podcast.title: Public Homosexuality Confession (1972)
podcast.body: On January 22, 1972, David Bowie made a shocking declaration to a British music tabloid reporter, stating, "I'm gay and I always have been." While such a statement is common today, in 1972, it was highly controversial and made him the first major rock and roll musician to publicly profess his homosexuality.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 9

podcast.title: Sexual Identity Declaration (1972)
podcast.body: Six months before the release of *The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust and The Spiders from Mars*, David Bowie declared himself to be gay. Given that homosexuality had only been decriminalized in England in 1967, this public confession from a major pop star had a huge liberating effect on individuals afraid to reveal their own sexual orientation. "Six months before the album came, a Bowie declared himself to be gay."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Top of the Pops Performance (July 6, 1972)
podcast.body: Bowie's seminal performance on Top of the Pops on July 6, 1972, with The Spiders from Mars, was highly influential. Dressed in a quilted jumpsuit, red boxing boots with green laces, and bright red-orange hair, Bowie's anisocoria (permanently dilated pupil from a childhood fight) added to his "otherworldly look." His public display of affection towards guitarist Mick Ronson (draping his arm around his shoulders) was considered "super duper gay" for the era and had a profound impact, leading to the immediate appearance of "Ziggy Clones" and helping young people feel accepted in their sexuality. "One especially interesting performance was on top of the pops on the BBC, July 6th, 1972."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

podcast.title: Ziggy Stardust Debut (February 1972)
podcast.body: David Bowie formally debuted the Ziggy Stardust character on February 10, 1972, at the Torquay Jug Pub in London. At the time, he was still a minor pop star, resulting in low attendance, but this performance marked the beginning of Ziggy's ascent. "Then on February 10th, 1972, David Bowie debuted the Ziggy character at the Torey Jug Pub in London."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

podcast.title: "Bowie Quits" Concert (July 3, 1973)
podcast.body: At the Hammersmith Odeon in London, Bowie staged a theatrical "retirement" for his Ziggy Stardust character, announcing that it was "the last show that we'll ever do." This event was captured by documentary filmmaker D.A. Pennebaker. Despite the dramatic announcement, Bowie did not actually quit, returning to the stage for a TV special less than two months later and continuing his recording and touring career. "Of all the shows on this tour, this particular show will remain with us the longest because not only is it the last show of the tour, but it's the last show that we'll ever do."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Equipment Theft by Steve Jones (July 1973)
podcast.body: During a multi-night stand at the Hammersmith Odeon in London in July 1973, David Bowie and The Spiders from Mars had microphones and amplifiers stolen by a young thief named Steve Jones, who later became the guitarist for the Sex Pistols. It is speculated that this stolen gear was used by the Sex Pistols in their early rehearsals and gigs in 1975, contributing to the punk rock era. "When Bowie and the spiders from Mars loaded into the Hammersmith Odien in London in July 1973 for a multi-night stand, a young thief named Steve Jones broke into the theatre and made off with a bunch of microphones and amplifiers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

podcast.title: Killing Off Ziggy Stardust (1973)
podcast.body: At the end of the 1973 Ziggy Stardust tour, Bowie announced to the audience that it would be "the last show that we'll ever do." While the public thought he was retiring, Bowie intended to retire the Ziggy persona to make way for a new one, Aladdin Sane. This willingness to "kill himself off" and constantly reinvent was admired by punks. "What he really meant though was that he was killing off Ziggy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Prolific Output and Reinvention (1973-1975)
podcast.body: Between 1973 and 1975, Bowie released an astonishing six albums in just three years and two months, including "Aladdin Sane," "Pin Ups," "Diamond Dogs," "David Live," and "Young Americans." Each record was different, making every release an event and keeping audiences guessing what Bowie would do next. "Album after album, single after single character after character two or after two or it was absolutely incredible."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Steve Jones' Theft of Bowie's Gear (July 3, 1973)
podcast.body: Following Bowie's final Ziggy Stardust show at the Hammersmith Odeon in London on July 2, 1973, a young thief named Steve Jones (who would later form The Sex Pistols) broke into the venue. While a night watchman slept, Jones stole microphones, amps, and cymbals, some of which would be used to start his new band. "A young thief named Steve Jones somehow got inside and managed to help himself to whatever he could carry out, mostly some microphones and some amps along with a couple of symbols."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ambitious Diamond Dogs Tour (1974)
podcast.body: The tour accompanying the "Diamond Dogs" album was one of the most ambitious rock had ever seen at the time. It featured elaborate sets, frequent costume changes, complex choreography, and a cherry picker boom that lifted Bowie over the audience during "Space Oddity." This hugely expensive and complex spectacle was groundbreaking, taking the basic rock and roll show to unprecedented levels of theater and spectacle, and audiences loved it. "The tour they came with the Diamond Dogs album was one of the most ambitious things Rock had ever seen."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ambitious Diamond Dogs Tour (1974)
podcast.body: The tour supporting the "Diamond Dogs" album was one of the most ambitious and expensive rock had ever seen. It featured elaborate sets, costume changes, choreography, and a cherry-picker boom that took Bowie out over the audience during "Space Oddity." This pushed the basic rock and roll show into unprecedented theatrical territory. "It was hugely expensive and very complex for its day and no one had ever seen anything like it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Cocaine Addiction and Paranoia in Los Angeles (1974-1976)
podcast.body: Between 1974 and 1976, Bowie was deeply entrenched in cocaine and alcohol addiction, a state exacerbated by his move to Los Angeles, the "cocaine capital of North America." This led to severe cocaine-induced paranoia, a common reaction among users, with Bowie's focus on witches. "Between 1974 and sometime in 1976, Bowie was an absolute mess."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Groundbreaking Diamond Dogs Tour (1974)
podcast.body: The tour supporting the "Diamond Dogs" album was one of the most ambitious and expensive rock had ever seen. It featured elaborate sets, costume changes, choreography, and a cherry-picker boom that took Bowie out over the audience during "Space Oddity." This pushed the basic rock and roll show into unprecedented theatrical territory. "It was hugely expensive and very complex for its day and no one had ever seen anything like it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Obsession with Witches and Bodily Fluids (1974-1976)
podcast.body: During his period of intense drug use and paranoia, Bowie became convinced that "witches" were trying to steal his "precious bodily fluids." To prevent this, he began saving all his urine in a fridge and maintained a strict diet of bell peppers and milk to keep his "essence pure," leading his weight to drop below 90 pounds. "Specifically, he got it into his mind that witches, that's as specific as we can get, were out to steal Bowie's precious bodily fluids."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Unrecorded Eccentricities (1974-1976)
podcast.body: The period between 1974 and 1976 saw David Bowie engage in "hundreds" of eccentric and costly endeavors, frequently spending millions on what were considered "truly stupid things." Much of this information remains undocumented in his official biographies because Bowie himself, due to his mental state at the time, could not recall many of these activities or purchases. "quedaron un montón por no decir cientos de estentricidades de David Bogud y esa etapa del 74 a 76 en el cual se gastaba ténticas millonadas en cosas verdaderamente estúpidas."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Pedro y el lobo de David Bowie

podcast.title: Bitter Split from Tony DeFries (April 1975)
podcast.body: Following Bowie's decision to split from Tony DeFries, a 48-hour marathon negotiation took place in April 1975 to finalize his departure. The terms of the split were so harsh that it's said Bowie broke down and cried at the conference table, remaining in shock for a week. The agreement stipulated that Bowie could leave only if Main Man took half of his earnings from albums dating back to *Hunky Dory* in 1971 through an upcoming live album, and DeFries was guaranteed 16% of Bowie's gross earnings for the next seven years, through to 1982.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: British Punk Favorite - 1975
podcast.body: By 1975, Bowie had become a favorite among British punks, who admired not only his music but also his non-status quo fashion sense and his defiant attitude. His influence was so strong that it was difficult to find a punk enthusiast in London who wasn't also a Bowie fan. "By 1975, he'd become a favorite among British punks."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mainstream Crossover Success (1975)
podcast.body: By 1975, with the "Young Americans" album, Bowie had become a global superstar whose music transcended genre boundaries. His songs were played on both Top 40 and rock radio stations, and he was considered cool in punk clubs. Tracks like "Fame" or "Young Americans" were even mixed in among dance music in disco clubs. "He was one of the biggest stars in the world."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Severe Addiction and Health Crisis - 1975-1976
podcast.body: During the period from late 1975 to late 1976, Bowie was heavily drinking and consuming tremendous amounts of cocaine, while subsisting on little more than milk and peppers. His weight plummeted to less than 90 pounds, indicating a severe health crisis, and he was described as "cracking up." "Bowie was drinking very heavily and using tremendous amounts of cocaine while eating a little more than milk and peppers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Artistic Integrity vs. Commercial Pressure (1976)
podcast.body: Faced with RCA's reluctance to release "Low" as he intended, Bowie refused to compromise his artistic vision by adding more commercial hits. The opposition from his label and managers ironically solidified his belief that he was heading in the right artistic direction, seeking to create music he loved rather than prioritizing assured commercial success.

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: David Bowie: La trilogía de Berlin 2

podcast.title: Berlin Regeneration and Routine (Late 1976)
podcast.body: In West Berlin, David Bowie rented an apartment at 155 Hauptstrasse in the Schöneberg district, situated above a car repair shop. He established a routine that included having breakfast at a gay bar next door and exploring the city's unique areas by walking or biking. Following a heart attack scare in the fall of 1976, both Bowie and Iggy Pop began to earnestly clean up their lifestyles, leading to a period of intense creativity. "Apparently, Bowie also had a big thing for Hitler and spent a lot of his time touring World War II sites."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 8

podcast.title: Discovery of Devo (1976)
podcast.body: In the summer of 1976, while in New York, David Bowie discovered the band Devo, a pivotal moment that would lead to his later involvement in their career.

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: David Bowie: La trilogía de Berlin 2

podcast.title: Drug Addiction and Mental Health Issues (1976)
podcast.body: In 1976, David Bowie was suffering from a severe drug addiction that was significantly impacting his mental health. This condition made him unable to enjoy the success of his album *Station to Station*. "Sufre una fuerte adicción a las drogas, las cuales están afectando a su salud mental."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: El proyecto que salvó a David Bowie. La trilogía de Berlín

podcast.title: Drug Addiction and Personal Decline (Pre-1976)
podcast.body: David Bowie suffered from a severe drug addiction and numerous other personal and professional problems, which he had been experiencing since the release and extensive tour of *Ziggy Stardust*. This progressive degeneration, culminating in 1976, was not always evident to the public due to his continued creative output of "very interesting" and "very good" projects like *Young Americans*. "David Bowie tiene un gravísimo problema de edición a las drogas casi desde el Pin-Avs. Y no sólo las drogas sino que David Bowie entra en una etapa en una de generación progresiva de muchas maneras, a que culminan en 1976."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: David Bowie: La trilogía de Berlin 1

podcast.title: Geographic Mobility (1976)
podcast.body: During the period of the Berlin Trilogy, Bowie did not live exclusively in Berlin. He traveled continuously between New York, Los Angeles, Geneva, and Paris. This constant movement contributed to the fragmented recording process of "Low."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: David Bowie: La trilogía de Berlin 2

podcast.title: Guest on Dina Shore Show (1976)
podcast.body: David Bowie appeared as a guest on Dina Shore's talk show in 1976, sharing an episode with Rosemary Clooney and Iggy Pop. "She literally had rosemary cluny on the same episode that she had David Bowie and Iggy pop."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
For the Record - The 70s

podcast.title: Legal and Personal Challenges (1976)
podcast.body: Bowie's frequent travels to places like Paris were partly due to legal issues related to changes in his management and the handling of his finances. He was also undergoing separation proceedings from his wife during this time.

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: David Bowie: La trilogía de Berlin 2

podcast.title: Move to Berlin for Recovery (1976)
podcast.body: To recover from his drug addiction and escape the intense spotlight of Los Angeles, David Bowie decided to move away. After a temporary stop in Switzerland, he relocated to Berlin with his friend Iggy Pop. "Para recuperarse y escapar del foco de atención, decide huir de los ángeles que su amigo y hip-hop."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: El proyecto que salvó a David Bowie. La trilogía de Berlín

podcast.title: Move to West Berlin for Sobriety (Post-1976)
podcast.body: Following his period of intense drug addiction and paranoia, Bowie, along with Iggy Pop, made a conscious decision to move to West Berlin to get sober, clean up, and dry out, seeking clarity from his drug-induced state. "It wasn't until he and Iggy Pop had a moment of clarity and decided that they needed to move to West Berlin to clean up, get sober and dry out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Nomadic Lifestyle (Pre-1976)
podcast.body: Prior to moving to Berlin, David Bowie adopted a nomadic lifestyle, continuously changing residences between cities such as New York, Paris, Switzerland, and Los Angeles. This restless existence indicated a person already "practically out of control." "Ya llega un punto en que David Bowie no vive en ningún sitio concreto. Pasa temporadas, en Nueva York, pasas temporadas en París, pasas temporadas en Suiza, pasas temporadas en Los Ángeles, está continuamente cambiando residencia."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: David Bowie: La trilogía de Berlin 1

podcast.title: Personal Transformation (1976)
podcast.body: David Bowie underwent a detoxification process in 1976, transforming from an eccentric, paranoid, and vain individual into a much more humble and discreet person, experiencing a profound catharsis and internal purification.

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: David Bowie: La trilogía de Berlin 2

podcast.title: Post-1976 Influence on Goth
podcast.body: David Bowie's music, particularly everything he released after 1976, played a role in coalescing the darker-minded punk scene, influencing the emergence of goth. His glam-era style from ten years prior was also a significant inspiration at The Batcave club. "This is where David Bowie turns up again, especially everything he released after 1976."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Recording of Peter and the Wolf Narration (1976)
podcast.body: In 1976, at the height of his mystical and esthetic ravings, Bowie conceived the idea to record Sergei Prokofiev's classical work *Peter and the Wolf*. He traveled to Philadelphia, where he hired the Philadelphia Symphony Orchestra, described as one of the most expensive orchestras in the world, to record the score while he narrated the children's story in a studio. This project took place during one of the most personally distressing periods of his life. "pensó que es una día de puta madre cogerse a la sinfónica de filadelfia que es una de las sinfónicas más caras del mundo y que grabas en la obra clásica de procofía Pedro y el Loco mientras leí al libro el cuento para niños el Pedro y el Loco."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Pedro y el lobo de David Bowie

podcast.title: Recording of Peter and the Wolf Narration (1976)
podcast.body: During his eccentric period in Switzerland, David Bowie recorded an orchestral version of Prokofiev's *Peter and the Wolf*, with himself narrating the story. This project illustrates his "un poco falla" (a bit off) mental state at the time. "La paranoia está que hizo David Bowie sobre Pedro y el obo de Procofir, en el cual grabó a un orquesto tocando Pedro y el obo y él se grababa narrando el cuento de Pedro y el obo, es justo de esta época."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: David Bowie: La trilogía de Berlin 1

podcast.title: Rehabilitation and Recording Low (1976)
podcast.body: After his tumultuous period in Geneva, David Bowie began rehabilitation in July 1976, marking a shift away from his extreme eccentricities. Following this period, he commenced recording the album *Low*, signifying a new artistic direction. "en enero del 76 es cuando se ha cinebra y en julio a bosto es cuando le digo un yacojizo le llavar el yacoja empieza a rehabilitar si se olvidara de todo esto empieza a grabar la famosa tecnología de la clín."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Pedro y el lobo de David Bowie

podcast.title: Struggles and Move to West Berlin (May 1976)
podcast.body: Living in Los Angeles had severely impacted David Bowie's sanity, leaving him in a fog of alcohol and cocaine abuse. He developed severe paranoia, believing aliens were coming to collect him, and reportedly collected his urine in jars as protection against alien abduction. Recognizing the need for a change, Bowie moved to West Berlin in late May 1976 with Iggy Pop to detoxify and regenerate amidst the city's bohemian and unconventional inhabitants. "Living in LA had seriously jeopardized their sanity."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 8

podcast.title: The Thin White Duke Persona - 1976
podcast.body: The "Station to Station" era was defined by Bowie's "Thin White Duke" persona, a character described as hollow, amoral, emotionless, and damaged, yet elegantly dressed in a white shirt and waistcoat. "Station to Station was the era of his thin white duke face."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Turbulent Year of 1976
podcast.body: The year 1976 was an extremely turbulent period in David Bowie's life, characterized by severe drug addiction that brought him close to death. His intense drug problem escalated significantly after he purchased a multi-million-dollar house in Geneva and moved there in the summer of 1976. "1976 fue el año un poco más turbio de la vida de David Bowie y la cuando estaba extremadamente drogadito y estaba rato y antes muriéndose."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Pedro y el lobo de David Bowie

podcast.title: Collaboration with Iggy Pop in Berlin (1977)
podcast.body: David Bowie was in Berlin with Iggy Pop in 1977, during which time Iggy Pop was "cleaning up and drying out and detoxing," and the song "Lust for Life" was created. "The track dates back to 1977 when Iggy was cleaning up and drying out and detoxing in Berlin with his buddy David Bowie."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mobility During Heroes Recording (1977)
podcast.body: Even during the recording of "Heroes" in Berlin, David Bowie maintained his highly mobile lifestyle, frequently entering and leaving the city. This transient presence contributed to the rapid completion of the album.

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: David Bowie: La trilogía de Berlin 2

podcast.title: Personal and Career Reset in Berlin (1977)
podcast.body: Prompted by his raging addiction and a need to change his trajectory, Bowie left America and England for West Berlin in 1977. There, with friend Iggy Pop, he aimed to kick drugs and record new music, leading to his prolific "Berlin period" with Brian Eno and Tony Visconti. "This finally prompted a personal and career reset for Boey, and he felt compelled to leave America and even England to change his trajectory."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Return of Vain Persona (1977)
podcast.body: Following the critical and commercial success of "Heroes," Bowie's self-confidence surged. He began to revert to a more grandiose and sometimes vain persona, contrasting sharply with the humbler demeanor he exhibited in 1976 after his detoxification. This shift led to growing discrepancies in his collaborations.

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: David Bowie: La trilogía de Berlin 2

podcast.title: Touring as Iggy Pop's Keyboardist (1977)
podcast.body: Instead of promoting his album *Low*, David Bowie chose to tour as a keyboardist for Iggy Pop, deliberately staying in the background. "Se negó a promocionarlo, bien su lugar se fue de girar como teclista el Diggy Pop, intentando quedar siempre en un segundo plano."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: El proyecto que salvó a David Bowie. La trilogía de Berlín

podcast.title: Departure from Berlin (Early 1978)
podcast.body: From early 1978 onwards, David Bowie no longer spent much time living or visiting Berlin, marking a physical and later inspirational detachment from the city. "Desde casi primeros es el 78 de David Bowie ya no pasaba mucho tiempo en Berlín y va a haber visita pasaba poco tiempo."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: David Bowie: La trilogía de Berlin 3

podcast.title: Rehabilitation and Return to Confidence (Mid-1978)
podcast.body: By mid-1978, David Bowie had completely rehabilitated, regaining much self-confidence after overcoming previous struggles. "A mitad de 1978, David Bowie ya estaba completamente rehabilitado, era una persona que había ganado otra vez mucha confianza en sí misma."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: David Bowie: La trilogía de Berlin 3

podcast.title: Post-Berlin Trilogy Move to New York (1979)
podcast.body: Following his productive period in Berlin, David Bowie moved to New York in 1979. "Después de su época en Berling, Bowie se trasladó a Nueva York en 1979."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: El proyecto que salvó a David Bowie. La trilogía de Berlín

podcast.title: "Ashes to Ashes" Music Video (1980)
podcast.body: The music video for "Ashes to Ashes" was a colorful, high-concept, and very expensive production, reportedly costing a quarter million pounds. It premiered on the BBC's "Top of the Pops" and contributed significantly to the single becoming David Bowie's fastest-selling UK single ever. "Promoted with a colorful, high concept and very expensive music video that premiered on the BBC's Top of the Pops and was reported to have cost a quarter million pounds."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: "Scary Monsters" Video (1980) - New Romantic Catalyst
podcast.body: David Bowie co-directed a groundbreaking video for a song from his "Scary Monsters" album in 1980, which notably used the Quantel Paintbox for special effects. Shot at Beechie Head in East Sussex, the video was a dream sequence featuring Bowie as a clown, an astronaut (referencing Ziggy Stardust and the movie Alien), and a mental patient, with costuming inspired by "The Sound of Music." Extras from London's avant-garde Blitz Club, including Steve Strange (later of Visage), contributed to its distinctive look. Costing $65,000 ($250,000 today), this surreal and fashionable video helped launch the New Romantic movement of the early 1980s. "Bowie's surreal but very fashionable clown character helped jumpstart the whole new romantic movement of the early 1980s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Future of the Music Video - Part 1

podcast.title: Major Tom's Return - "Ashes to Ashes" (1980)
podcast.body: Bowie revived his beloved character Major Tom in the lead single for "Scary Monsters," portraying him as a "doomed astronaut" aimlessly knocking through space while "strung out on a kind of galactic heroine." This cheeky continuation of the character's story was a key element of the single's UK success. "Maybe that was because on its lead single, Bowie was reviving his most beloved character, Major Tom."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: "Cat People" Production Discontent (1982)
podcast.body: David Bowie was unhappy with Giorgio Moroder's production of "Cat People (Putting Out Fire)," despite critics calling it one of Bowie's best vocal performances. This discontent led him to ask Nile Rogers to re-record the track with a "crunchier" backing for his subsequent album. "However, David Bowie was unhappy with Moroder's production, and he asked the producer of his next album, Nile Rogers, to re-record Cat People with a new, crunchier backing track."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: "The Young Ones" Satirical Gag (1982)
podcast.body: The widespread cultural phenomenon of "Ashes to Ashes" in the UK led to references in popular media, including a throwaway gag on the satirical British punk comedy show "The Young Ones" a couple of years after its release, highlighting its pervasive recognition. "Ashes to Ashes was a true UK phenomenon, the kind that invited injuks, such as this throwaway gag, a couple of years later, on the satirical British punk comedy show The Young Ones."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Nile Rogers Collaboration Origin (1982)
podcast.body: David Bowie met Nile Rogers, the former mastermind of disco band Chic, at a New York club in 1982 and invited him to write and record in Montreux, Switzerland. Bowie sought Rogers to shake up his sound after leaving RCA, explicitly stating he wanted to record the biggest hits of his career. "David Bowie had met Nile Rogers, former mastermind of disco band Sheik, at a New York club in 1982, and he invited Nile to write and record with him in Montreux, Switzerland."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: "China Girl" Music Video Controversy (1983)
podcast.body: The music video for "China Girl" was considered risque, satirizing Asian stereotypes and concluding with Bowie and actress Geeling Ng recreating the fully nude crashing waves embrace from the 1950s film "From Here to Eternity." The controversy surrounding the video likely contributed to the song's commercial success. "fueled by a risque music video that satirized Asian stereotypes and closed with Bowie recreating the crashing waves embrace from the 50s film from here to eternity, with actress Gilling Eng, both fully nude in the surf."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: "China Girl" Royalties for Iggy Pop (1983)
podcast.body: Bowie's decision to cover "China Girl," a song he co-wrote for Iggy Pop's 1977 album "The Idiot," was partly an act of friendship. Iggy Pop's finances were described as "shaky" in the early 80s, and Bowie knew the royalties from the hit cover would provide a significant windfall for him. "Legend has it, Bowie wanted to do his friend Iggy Pop a favor by covering the song. Iggy's finances in the early 80s were shaky, and Bowie knew the royalties from a China Girl cover would be a windfall."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: "Let's Dance" Birth from Acoustic Guitar (1983)
podcast.body: The massive hit "Let's Dance" originated from a simple tune Bowie had written on an acoustic guitar. Nile Rogers then transformed it by adding syncopation, turning it into a "bang" and a signature glossy new romantic new wave track. "Rogers took a simple tune Bowie had written on an acoustic guitar, added syncopation, and turned it into a bang."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: "Serious Moonlight" Tour Image (1983)
podcast.body: During his "Serious Moonlight" tour, captured in the "Modern Love" music video, Bowie appeared as a sleek, "up-ified pop idol," dressed in a yellow suit with blonde hair teased into a Little Richard-style pompadour. This image was part of his mid-80s "imperial phase" persona, reflecting his embrace of mainstream pop stardom. "captured Bowie live on stage on his just launched Sirius Moonlight tour, Natalie dressed in a yellow suit, his blonde hair teased into a little Richard style pompadour, tricked out like a sleek, up-ified pop idol."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: $17.5 Million EMI Record Deal - 1983
podcast.body: In 1983, Bowie secured a monumental $17.5 million record deal with EMI Records, one of the largest in the industry at that time. In exchange, he committed to creating a more commercially accessible album. "And then there was the new 17.5 million dollar record deal with EMI Records, one of the biggest deals in the industry to that time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: $17.5 Million EMI Record Deal - 1983
podcast.body: In the 1980s, Bowie signed a new record deal with EMI Records worth $17.5 million, one of the biggest deals in the music industry at that time. This substantial contract influenced his decision to create a more commercially oriented album like "Let's Dance." "And then there was the new 17.5 million dollar record deal with EMI Records, one of the biggest deals in the industry to that time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: MTV Racism Challenge (1983)
podcast.body: In 1983, David Bowie confronted MTV VJ Mark Goodman in an interview, calling out the channel's "subtle racism" for featuring very few Black artists, particularly during prime daytime hours. He observed that while many Black artists were making excellent videos, they were rarely aired on MTV, in contrast to a dedicated Black music station. "I'm just flawed by the fact that there's so many so few black artists featured on it. Why is that?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Future of the Music Video - Part 1

podcast.title: The Hunger (1983) Role
podcast.body: David Bowie starred as an elegant vampire in the 1983 movie *The Hunger*, which became a favorite among Goth enthusiasts. The film also featured a nightclub scene with Bauhaus performing "Bela Lugosi's Dead." "Bowie starred as a rather elegant vampire in a movie called The Hunger back in 1983."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Critically Panned but Chart-Successful Material (1984-1985)
podcast.body: During his "imperial phase" in 1984 and 1985, Bowie released material, like the album "Tonight" and single "Blue Jean," that was critically panned yet performed exceptionally well on the charts. Bowie himself later apologized for the quality of "Tonight," indicating his ambivalence about this period. "In 1984 and 85 Bowie released lackluster, critically panned material that did well on the charts anyway."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: "Dancing in the Street" Music Video (1985)
podcast.body: The music video for the "Dancing in the Street" duet with Mick Jagger was shot hastily on a movie set backlot in a single night and became known as a "laugh riot." It featured Bowie and Jagger shouting lyrics and performing "hokey dad dancing," which made them appear to be "maybe flirting with each other." "The music video, in particular, shot on a movie sets back lot in a rush on a single night, was a laugh riot."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: "Airless Digital Rock" Criticism (1987)
podcast.body: Bowie's attempt to rock harder with the "Never Let Me Down" album in 1987 resulted in a sound described by critics and fans as "airless digital rock," indicating a failure to satisfy either rock or pop fans and leaving a "bad taste" in Bowie's mouth. "But when the album arrived, neither critics nor fans came away impressed with Bowie's airless digital rock."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Tin Machine Identity Struggle (1989-1992)
podcast.body: Despite generating hits on the modern rock chart, Tin Machine never developed a personality beyond its status as "David Bowie's side project." The albums' poor sales, with the debut not even going gold, ultimately led Bowie back to his solo career. "While Tin Machine's workmen like Alt Rock proved decent radio fodder, the band never developed a personality beyond its status as David Bowie's side project."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Tin Machine as a Response to Art Punk (1989)
podcast.body: Bowie formed Tin Machine as a deliberate move away from pop, submerging his identity into a "grungy rock band" with a metallic, feedback-laden sound. This was his direct response to the rising art punk sound of bands like Pixies and Sonic Youth, showcasing his commitment to noisier, more experimental rock. "It was his response to the rising art punk sound of bands like the Pixies or Sonic Youth."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Charismatic Interview Subject (1990, Tin Machine era)
podcast.body: In 1990, during his Tin Machine years, David Bowie exhibited a profound level of charisma in an interview, similar to Bono. He maintained intense eye contact, creating an immersive experience for the interviewer, who was so overwhelmed that they forgot to record the conversation. Years later, when reminded of the incident, Bowie directly yet humorously acknowledged the error. "The only other person with that level of charisma that I ever talked to was David Bowie."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 1000th Episode of the Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Lost Interview Tape (1990)
podcast.body: In 1990, prior to the ongoing history show, the speaker had a 30-minute, face-to-face interview with David Bowie during his Tin Machine years. The speaker was so overwhelmed by Bowie's presence, focusing on his various personas, that he forgot to unpause his tape machine, resulting in no recording. "And I don't remember what I asked him. I don't remember what he said because I was just like, this is Bowie."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: OGHONM 1000th Episode: The Q&A From the Live Recording

podcast.title: Naked in Bed with Mick Jagger – Angela Bowie's 1990 TV Claim, Denied Then Partially Walked Back
podcast.body: On May 4, 1990, David Bowie's ex-wife Angela appeared on the Joan Rivers Show, newly freed from a 10-year gag order after their divorce. She stated on national television: "I caught him in bed with Mick Jagger — and yes, they were naked." Bowie was a professed bisexual during the 1970s. Mick Jagger immediately dismissed the claim as "rubbish," and Bowie's lawyer sent an open letter stating that "any implication that there was ever a gay affair between Mick Jagger and David Bowie is an absolute fabrication." Within a week, Angela was qualifying her statement. By her 1993 autobiography, the account had evolved: she had walked in, assumed they had been having sex, and that was her honest belief, but she had no proof. An additional complication: Angela may have had her own affair with Jagger during the marriage, possibly inspiring the Rolling Stones song "Angie" — or, in another rumor, that "Angie" referred to David himself using a nickname. "Did they spend the night together? Yes. Were they naked? Apparently. Was it sexual? Who knows?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rumored Affair with Mick Jagger (1990)
podcast.body: A long-standing rumor regarding an affair between David Bowie and Mick Jagger originated on the Joan Rivers show on May 4, 1990. Angela Bowie, David's ex-wife (married 1970-1980), claimed on the show, after a decade-long gag order from her divorce settlement expired, that she caught them naked in bed together. Bowie had professed bisexuality in the 1970s, which lent some credibility to the story. Mick Jagger vehemently denied the claims, and Bowie's lawyer issued a letter calling any implication of a gay affair an "absolute fabrication." Angela Bowie later revised her story in her 1993 autobiography, stating she "just assumed they were having sex" and lacked proof. "I caught David in bed with Mick Jagger."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Financial Freedom - Post-1996
podcast.body: After his problematic contract with former manager Tony DeFrees finally expired in 1996, all royalties from Bowie's music began flowing directly to him, granting him the financial freedom to make music on his own terms once again. "Remember that bad deal with his old manager, Tony DeFrees? It expired in 1996, and all royalties from Bowie's music started flowing to Bowie."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Online Chat Stunt (1996)
podcast.body: During an online chat in September 1996 for the release of "Telling Lies," Bowie engaged in a playful deception where three people pretended to be him. Fans were asked to vote on the real Bowie, and according to one account, the actual Bowie finished third. "At the end of it, fans were asked to vote on which of the three Bowies was the real one."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 50th Birthday Concert (1997)
podcast.body: Bowie celebrated his 50th birthday by throwing a concert at Madison Square Garden, joined on stage by prominent alt-rockers such as Sonic Youth, Foo Fighters, The Cure's Robert Smith, and Lou Reed, demonstrating his continued relevance and connections within the alternative music scene, even if his 50s became his quietest artistic period. "Earthling arrived just a few weeks after a 50th birthday concert Bowie threw himself at Madison Square Garden joined on stage by such alt rockers as Sonic Youth, Foo Fighters, The Cures Robert Smith and Old Friend and Alt Rock Godfather Lou Reed."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Bowie Bonds (1997) – Financial Innovation
podcast.body: In 1997, Bowie, with banker David Pullman, pioneered "Bowie Bonds," a financial instrument where he securitized his future music royalties as collateral to issue bonds. He sold these bonds, raising $55 million, which he then used to repurchase the rights to his music that he had lost through previous bad management deals with Tony DeFries. This marked the first time a performer used their cash flow potential in this manner. Issued a few years before widespread music piracy, the bonds initially had a high A3 rating and paid 7.9% interest over 10 years, attracting Prudential Insurance. However, within 18 months, the music industry tanked due to Napster and declining physical sales, causing the bonds' rating to drop to BAA3 (near junk status). In 2007, the bonds were liquidated, and all music rights reverted to Bowie, meaning by his death in 2016, he owned almost everything he had produced. "This was the first time in financial history that a performer had used their cash flow potential to make money."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bowie Bonds (1997) – Financial Innovation
podcast.body: In 1997, Bowie collaborated with New York investment banker David Pullman to create "Bowie Bonds," a package of securities backed by the future projected royalties of 25 Bowie albums (287 songs recorded before 1990). Bowie received $55 million upfront, using the money to buy back rights he had lost to his former manager. This was a pioneering use of intellectual property to secure a financial instrument. "In 1997, a New York investment banker named David Pullman put together a package of securities backed by the future projected royalties of 25 Bowie albums, a total of 287 songs that were recorded before 1990."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bowie Net (1997-2006) – Pioneering ISP
podcast.body: Over a couple of years, Bowie and a small team created Bowie Net, launched around 1997-1998, which functioned as an internet service provider. Subscribers paid $20 a month for internet access and a @DavidBowie.com email address, or $6 for access to exclusive content like songs, music videos, chat rooms, images of his paintings, and journal writings. Bowie was known to lurk anonymously in chat rooms. In 1999, it held a song contest with 80,000 lyric submissions, won by Alex Grant whose lyrics appeared on the *Hours* album. It featured LiveAndWell.com for live tracks and Bowie World, a 3D virtual environment where users could navigate a Bowie-themed city as avatars and communicate with other fans. At its peak in 1999, Bowie Net had 100,000 customers but ceased operations in 2006 as larger companies copied his innovations. "Bowie Net was incredibly ahead of its time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Creation of Bowie Bonds (1997)
podcast.body: In 1997, David Bowie, in collaboration with investment banker David Pullman, created a financial instrument called "Bowie Bonds." This involved securitizing 287 songs from 25 albums recorded before 1990, effectively making them asset-backed securities. In exchange for forfeiting 10 years of royalty income, Bowie received an immediate lump sum payment of $55 million. He utilized this money to repurchase the rights to songs he had lost to his former manager, Tony DeFrees. "David Bowie and an investment banker named David Pullman created a financial instrument called Bowie Bonds. To use Wall Street speak, 287 songs from 25 albums recorded before 1990 became asset-backed securities. In exchange for forfeiting royalty income for a period of 10 years, Bowie received an immediate payment of $55 million. He used that money to buy out the rights to songs he lost to his former manager, Tony DeFrees."

podcast.title: Secret Comeback (2011-2013)
podcast.body: Bowie orchestrated his 2013 comeback album, *The Next Day*, in absolute secrecy. He worked with trusted producer Tony Visconti and a small coterie of musicians, all of whom signed non-disclosure agreements. His family and the skeleton staff at The Magic Shop studio (near his apartment) kept the secret. He had minimal staff, only his fiercely loyal personal assistant Coco Schwab and business person Bill Zysblat, with no pressure from his record label, Sony. His understanding of the internet meant he knew he could announce his return without a traditional marketing campaign, simply by dropping a hint online. "How did Bowie, one of the most famous musicians in the world that ever seen, manage that? He was working with Tony Visconti again. Tony can keep a secret."

This "ready-made art" implied Bowie was regarding his own life as an elder statesman with humor and skepticism, similar to how he satirized Major Tom in "Ashes to Ashes." "And when fans saw the album's cover, many thought Bowie was taking the piss. It was simply a copy of Bowie's 1977 Heroes album cover, a famous black and white photo of Bowie holding up two hands around his face in a kind of proto-vogue pose."

"He started work around 10 o'clock each day with a double macchiato from a coffee shop called La Colomb. And he finished up at a decenar of the day so he could be home for dinner with his wife and daughter."
