podcast.body: The production of Black Star was initially planned with three producers: David Bowie, Tony Visconti, and James Murphy. However, James Murphy, overwhelmed by other projects and unaware of Bowie's terminal illness, was often late or absent, didn't understand the material, and ultimately declined a full producer credit, contributing only specific rhythmic and sound elements. "Por desgracia la cosa salió muy mal."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Black Star as an Unheard Artwork
podcast.body: Despite its massive sales, especially posthumously, many buyers of Black Star may not actively listen to the album because of its complex art-jazz nature. It's suggested that many purchased it out of affection or as a farewell to the artist, rather than for regular listening, perhaps only engaging with a song like "Lazarus." "Resulta un tanto triste que mucha gente se ha comprado y no lo vaya a escuchar operativamente, no le escucha, al final es un disco de Arjas muy complejo que contrasta mucho con las ventas masivas que tiene."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Blue-Eyed Plastic Soul Singer
podcast.body: The "Young Americans" album introduced a new Bowie persona: the "blue-eyed plastic soul singer." This look featured a new haircut with a part on the right, baggy pants, and stylishly baggy sweatshirts, embodying a professed love for black music. This endorsement encouraged many of his fans to explore soul and R&B. "Young Americans introduced yet another Bowie. The blue-eyed plastic soul singer."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Blue-Eyed Plastic Soul Singer
podcast.body: During the "Diamond Dogs" tour, Bowie began transitioning from his "spaceman" image to a more elegant, sophisticated look with shorter hair and tailored suits. This paralleled a shift in his musical interests towards American soul and R&B, leading to the smoother, funkier sound of "Young Americans." This endorsement of black music encouraged many of his fans to explore those genres. "Bowie became less space man and more elegant, shorter hair, tailored suits, an air of sophistication."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bonds Downgraded Due to Internet Sales Decline
podcast.body: Despite their innovative nature, Bowie Bonds were downgraded to junk status by 2004, approximately seven years after their creation. This downgrade was a direct consequence of declining music sales brought on by the rise of the internet, an irony given Bowie's own prophecy about music becoming "cheap as water" due to internet distribution. "By 2004, about seven years in, those bonds were downgraded to junk status. Why? Well, because of declining music sales brought on by the rise of the internet."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bowie Bonds - Financial Innovation
podcast.body: In 1997, Bowie collaborated with New York investment banker David Pullman to create "Bowie Bonds," a package of securities backed by the future projected royalties of 25 Bowie albums (287 songs recorded before 1990). Bowie received $55 million upfront, using the money to buy back rights he had lost to his former manager. This was a pioneering use of intellectual property to secure a financial instrument. "In 1997, a New York investment banker named David Pullman put together a package of securities backed by the future projected royalties of 25 Bowie albums, a total of 287 songs that were recorded before 1990."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bowie's Foresight on Internet Disruption
podcast.body: At the time of the Bowie Bonds' creation, many considered his decision to forfeit royalties as "crazy." However, Bowie was studying the emerging internet and correctly predicted its disruptive impact on the music business, anticipating a decline in traditional record royalties, which materialized with the rise of Napster and file-sharing. "At the time, though, people thought that Bowie was crazy giving up his songs like this. But Bowie knew what was coming. He was studying this new thing called the Internet, and he knew that it was going to completely disrupt the music business, and he knew that old school record royalties were going to drop, which is exactly what happened, especially when Napster and all the other file-trading programs popped up."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bowie's Influence on Rock and Roll
podcast.body: David Bowie, particularly through his Ziggy Stardust alter ego, profoundly altered the trajectory of rock and roll's development and served as a powerful source of inspiration for countless aspiring rock musicians globally. "How Bowie and Ziggy changed the course of the development of rock and roll."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bowie's Listening Habits During Black Star Recording
podcast.body: David Bowie had a compulsive listening habit during the recording of Black Star. He became a huge follower of Börtshoff Canadá in his final years and listened to their music almost compulsively. He was also deeply fascinated by the hip hop trio Dead Grips and considered Kendrick Lamar's album *Tu Pimp a Butterfly* an "authentic masterpiece," which he listened to continuously as a major influence. "él se convierte un grandísimo seguidor de Börtshoff Canadá en los últimos años y escuchaba Börtshoff Canadá de manera casi compulsiva durante la grabación del Black Star."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Bowie's Reaction to Lost Tape Story
podcast.body: Years later, the speaker recounted the lost tape story to Bowie, who listened intently, placed his hands on the speaker's shoulders, and said, "well, that was stupid if he wasn't it." This was the last interaction they had. "And he's listening intently and he puts his hands on my shoulders and stares me in the eye and says, well, that was stupid if he wasn't it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: OGHONM 1000th Episode: The Q&A From the Live Recording

podcast.title: Bowie-esque Style
podcast.body: David Bowie is used as an example of an artist whose distinct approach to music inspires others, with artists often being described as "Bowie-esque" if their work conjures similar images. This illustrates the concept of artists building on the accomplishments of those who came before them. "How many times have you heard an artist describe this bowie-esque because their approach to music conjures images of what David Bowie did?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Box Set Demo Contributions
podcast.body: David Bowie has benefited from including demo versions in his box set collections, leveraging this format to release previously unheard material. "David Bowie, the cure, the jam, the remones, joy division, the velvet underground, the smashing pumpkins, they've all benefited from putting demo versions into their box set collections."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Brian Eno Collaboration
podcast.body: Brian Eno produced all three of David Bowie's Berlin records, a collaboration that further cemented Eno's reputation as one of the most innovative and important producers in the world. This partnership was crucial to the electronic sound and influential nature of the Berlin trilogy. "All three of David Bowie's Berlin records were produced by Brian Eno."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 8

podcast.title: British Rock Tradition
podcast.body: David Bowie was mentioned as part of the proud tradition of British rock and roll that needed to be saved from the "grunge marauders" invading from the US. "Her majesty's empire needed to be saved from the grunge marauders, the proud tradition of British rock and roll, the Beatles, the Stones, Led Zeppelin, Sexbistles, Clash, Bowie, it all needed to be saved from the likes of Nirvana and Pearl Jam and Soundgarden."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Broad Cultural Influence
podcast.body: Bowie's influence extends beyond music, impacting style, image, concert performance, fashion, film, stage, painting, museums, and even career management. His work significantly affected various music genres like rock, punk, new wave, goth, industrial, electronic music, dance, grunge, and indie rock. He is considered one of the most important figures for gay people in pop culture, with tremendous social and political implications, especially in the UK. "Bowie's influence can be found all over rock and punk and new wave, and goth, and industrial, and electronic music, dance, grunge, indie rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Broadway Success - The Elephant Man (Early 1980s)
podcast.body: Two and a half years before "Let's Dance" hit number one, Bowie played the title role in "The Elephant Man" on Broadway, breaking the record for a non-musical by selling out 125 performances. This demonstrated his versatility and widespread appeal beyond music. "Two and a half years ago, he played the title role in the Elephant Man, and he broke the Broadway record for a non-musical by selling out 125 performances."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Busy and Touring During Lodger Recordings
podcast.body: During the recording of *Lodger*, David Bowie was constantly busy and actively touring, making the recording process somewhat diffuse and complex. "Todo un poco difuso, David Bowie ya no paraba, ya estaba haciendo giras."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: David Bowie: La trilogía de Berlin 3

podcast.title: Cause of Death
podcast.body: Bowie had been quietly battling liver cancer, which ultimately took his life. "But the liver cancer he'd been battling quietly and out of sight finally took him."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 2: The Role of Indie Rock

podcast.title: Champion of Electronic Music
podcast.body: In the late 1970s, David Bowie, alongside producer and friend Brian Eno, championed electronic music pioneered by acts like Kraftwerk and Donna Summer. Bowie was not unfamiliar with synthesizers or dance beats. "And in the late 70s, it was David Bowie, and his producer and friend Brian Eno, who championed the electronic music being pioneered by the likes of Croftvark and Donna Summer."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Charisma Comparison
podcast.body: David Bowie is described as having a level of charisma comparable only to Bono. "The only other person with that level of charisma that I ever talked to was David Bowie."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: OGHONM 1000th Episode: The Q&A From the Live Recording

podcast.title: Chart Performance Disparity (UK vs. US) - 1970s
podcast.body: During his first decade of hit making, David Bowie's stardom differed considerably between his British homeland and America. In the US, he was a star, but in the UK, he was a mega star; several of his peak glam era LPs topped the British album chart, while none hit number one in America. His quirkier Berlin LPs consistently made the UK top five, but fell short of the top ten in America, which generally preferred his funk and soul excursions. "During his first decade of hit making, David Bowie's stardom in his British homeland, differed considerably from his chart performance in America."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Chess Enthusiast
podcast.body: David Bowie was known to play chess, a popular pastime for artists spending extensive time on the road. "That was certainly the case with David Bowie."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Claire Shenstone's Day Out with Bowie
podcast.body: During the recording of the *Heroes* album, Bowie spent a day with his then-girlfriend, model, and artist Claire Shenstone. The night before, Bowie had dreamt he was swimming with dolphins. The next day, they visited East Berlin and observed soldiers marching, an experience which Shenstone claims directly inspired the song's lyrics, specifically the references to dolphins, standing by the wall, and gunshots. "Shenstone claims that the song's lyrics were directly inspired by that day they spent together."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Classical Music Studies
podcast.body: During his esthetic phase in Geneva in 1976, Bowie decided to study classical music, hiring very expensive private teachers to guide him. This costly pursuit was part of a broader period of artistic experimentation and lavish spending, reflecting his erratic behavior at the time. "el decidió estudiar música clásica y se gastó un dinerad de profesores calísimos de música clásica."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Pedro y el lobo de David Bowie

podcast.title: Cocaine-Induced Haze of Mid-70s
podcast.body: The mid-1970s became a blur for Bowie due to a "cocaine-induced haze." This period heavily influenced his lyrics on the 'Station to Station' album, reflecting growing paranoia, and he later claimed not to remember anything about the album's creation due to his raging addiction. "This would become a theme for Boey over the next year, a cocaine-induced haze that made the mid-70s one long blur for him."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Collaboration on Lust for Life
podcast.body: After their tour, Bowie and Iggy Pop went to West Berlin and recorded Iggy's "Lust for Life" album in just 13 days. This quick, collaborative effort produced what remains the best work of Iggy's career. "Once that tour was over, the two of them went back to West Berlin, where they made another record for Iggy in just 13 days."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About Iggy Pop

podcast.title: Collaboration on The Idiot
podcast.body: Bowie was instrumental in Iggy Pop's first solo album, "The Idiot," starting work in June 1976 and completing it by March 1977. He played "everything else" on the album, while Iggy handled vocals, establishing a key creative partnership. "Then in June 1976 Bowie began working with Iggy on Iggy's first solo album. It was Iggy on vocals and Bowie on everything else."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About Iggy Pop

podcast.title: Collaboration with Alexander McQueen
podcast.body: David Bowie engaged in fashion collaborations, famously pairing with the designer Alexander McQueen, showcasing his involvement with high fashion and its integration into his artistic persona. "Meanwhile, David Bowie paired with Alexander McQueen."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Collaboration with Arcade Fire
podcast.body: David Bowie performed and recorded with Arcade Fire, highlighting the indie band's widespread recognition and influence across different music generations. "they performed a recorded with David Bowie."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Collaboration with Brian Eno and the Berlin Trilogy
podcast.body: During his recovery, Bowie also listened to Brian Eno's *Discreet Music*, which greatly influenced him. This led to their collaboration on Bowie's next three albums—*Low*, *Heroes*, and *Lodger*—which would become known as the Berlin Trilogy. "escuchado Discreet Music de Brian Inno, con quien crearía sus próximos tres discos, la que sería conocida como la trilogía de Berlin."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: El proyecto que salvó a David Bowie. La trilogía de Berlín

podcast.title: Collaboration with Brian Eno and the Berlin Trilogy
podcast.body: Brian Eno produced all three of David Bowie's Berlin records, a collaboration that further cemented Eno's reputation as one of the most innovative and important producers in the world. This partnership was crucial to the electronic sound and influential nature of the Berlin trilogy. "All three of David Bowie's Berlin records were produced by Brian Eno."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 8

podcast.title: Collaboration with John Lennon
podcast.body: By 1975, Bowie was famous enough that John Lennon was willing to collaborate, co-writing the song "Fame." Lennon, in the middle of his "lost weekend" separation from Yoko Ono, happily partied and worked with Bowie. Their professional and personal relationships extended to their associates, with Lennon's assistant, May Pang, eventually marrying Bowie's producer, Tony Visconti. "By this time Bowie was big enough that someone like John Lennon was willing to hang out and even do a little co-writing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Collaboration with Moby
podcast.body: David Bowie is listed among the important artists who collaborated with Moby after the success of *Play*, seeking his sounds, remixes, rhythmic bases, or commissioning compositions. "trabajando de una manera u otra con gente pues como David Bowie."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: MOBY · PLAY. Influencia absoluta de la música de gran consumo

podcast.title: Collaboration with Nile Rodgers
podcast.body: For his 1983 album "Let's Dance," David Bowie collaborated with Nile Rodgers, known as the driving force behind Chic, one of the notable disco bands of the late 1970s. This collaboration allowed Bowie to create a sound that blended alternative, post disco, and alt dance elements. "He was produced by Nile Rogers, the guy behind Sheik, one of the better disco bands in the late 1970s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Collaboration with Tony Visconti
podcast.body: Throughout most of his career, David Bowie worked closely with producer Tony Visconti. However, Visconti did not produce Bowie's glam music albums, specifically *Ziggy Stardust*, *Aladdin Sane*, or *Pin Ups*. During this period, Visconti was actively involved in producing albums for Marc Bolan's band T-Rex, contributing to the birth of glam music from another angle. "David Bowie trabajó casi toda su vida con un productor que se llama Tony Biz Conti."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: EL PIONERO DEL GLAM: MARC BOLAN Y T REX

podcast.title: Collapse Backstage at "Lazarus" Musical
podcast.body: In early December 2015, after attending a performance of his musical "Lazarus" and meeting with the director, Bowie collapsed backstage. He subsequently regained some strength and was seen on the streets of New York as late as his 69th birthday, January 8th, 2016. "In early December 2015, Bowie attended a performance of his musical Lazarus. After meeting with the director, he collapsed backstage."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Collision with Iggy Pop and The Velvet Underground
podcast.body: The narrative sets up a significant future "collision" of Bowie, Iggy Pop, and The Velvet Underground in New York. "And we'll spend some time in New York trying to figure out how Bowie, Iggy Pop and the Velvet Underground all collided in a very important way."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Concerts as Theater
podcast.body: With Ziggy Stardust, Bowie transformed rock concerts from mere performances by musicians standing on a low stage into theatrical spectacles. These shows incorporated choreography and elaborate costuming, making the concert an integral part of the "show" itself, blending hard rock with vaudeville, glitter pop with real theater, and fashion with technology. "Back then, concerts were basically a bunch of dude standing around on a low stage. But with Ziggy, the concert was theater, a spectacle with its choreography and costuming."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Confidence from "Space Oddity" Success
podcast.body: The success of "Space Oddity," particularly its high chart position in the UK, provided Bowie with much-needed confidence. This newfound self-assurance encouraged him to be even bolder with his experiments in image and presentation, leading to his iconic gender-bending styles. "This success gave Bowie some much needed confidence. He felt he could even be more bold with his experiments with the image and presentation, which often involves some serious gender bending."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Consequence of "Man Dress" Failure
podcast.body: The commercial and cultural failure of *The Man Who Sold the World*'s dress cover, which sold less than 1,400 copies in America in its first seven months, directly influenced Bowie's subsequent artistic direction. This setback prompted him to develop a more "palatable" character for American audiences, leading directly to the creation of Ziggy Stardust. "Bowie's gamble to wear a dress in public was such a failure that he immediately started thinking about how he could morph into something a little bit more palatable for American taste."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 1

podcast.title: Continued Support for Iggy Pop
podcast.body: Despite their paths diverging after the Berlin Trilogy, David Bowie consistently provided support to Iggy Pop, most notably through royalties from his cover of "China Girl," which helped Iggy Pop financially. He also collaborated on Iggy Pop's second album. "el propio David Bowie nunca habría terminado de darle cierto apoyo a Iguipop en ese sentido."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: David Bowie: La trilogía de Berlin 3

podcast.title: Correct Pronunciation of "Bowie"
podcast.body: The correct pronunciation of his adopted surname is "Bowie," not "Bowie" or "Bow-ee." Bowie himself affirmed this pronunciation, despite guitarist Mick Ronson and others sometimes mispronouncing it. "It should be pronounced Bowie. And trust me, I spoke to the man himself."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Covered by Peter Gabriel
podcast.body: David Bowie's music was included among the favorite artists covered by Peter Gabriel on his 2010 album, "Scratch My Back." "There was David Bowie and Paul Simon, Talking Hints, Lou Reed, Neil Young, Radiohead, and Arcade Fire."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Who the Hell is Arcade Fire? Part 2

podcast.title: Covered by Scott Weiland (Year Unknown)
podcast.body: David Bowie's music was covered by Scott Weiland on his album "A Compilation of Scott Weiland Cover Songs." "covering everything from the Smiths and David Bowie to Nirvana, the Flaming Lips, and even the Stone Roses."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Creation of Ziggy Stardust
podcast.body: Building on glam rock concepts, Bowie developed the character Ziggy Stardust. This persona was inspired by the outrageous behavior of Iggy Pop and The Stooges, the artsy "scummy" persona of Lou Reed and the Velvet Underground, the "god-alien" self-perception of Vince Taylor, and the "space travel obsessed" persona of Norman Odom, also known as the Legendary Stardust Cowboy. Bowie combined these influences, changing "Iggy" to "Ziggy" and adopting "Stardust" as the surname. "He invented an entire character completely rooted in glam rock concepts that borrowed from the outrageous behavior of another new friend, Iggy Pop... So Bowie, taking all this information, changed Iggy to Ziggy and adopted Stardust as a surname and thus Ziggy Stardust was born."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

podcast.title: Cremation and Ashes in Bali
podcast.body: Following his death on January 10th, 2016, Bowie's body was cremated. In his will, he requested that his ashes be scattered in Bali and stipulated that there should be no funeral. "His body was cremated, and he asked in his will that his ashes be scattered in Bali. He left instructions that there be no funeral."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Critical Decline in the 80s
podcast.body: During the mid-to-late 1980s, Bowie's music and performances, including albums like "Tonight" and "Never Let Me Down," and the "Glass Spiders tour," faced harsh criticism, with descriptions like "tired" and "fake enthusiasm" being used to characterize his work, suggesting a departure from his earlier innovative spirit. "Words like tired and phrases like fake enthusiasm were thrown around."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Cultural Impact - Redefining Rock Stardom
podcast.body: David Bowie profoundly changed culture by subverting the traditional meaning of a rock star, pushing music into new realms of theater and spectacle. His continuously shape-shifting style was widely imitated by artists like Madonna and Lady Gaga, and he served as a crucial inspiration for punk, new wave, post-punk, electronic, goth, industrial, and alternative movements, including bands like the Pixies, Nirvana, Nine Inch Nails, and Arcade Fire. "David Bowie irrevocably changed our culture. He began by subverting what it meant to be a rock star."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Departure from Hippie Culture
podcast.body: Ziggy Stardust marked a distinct departure from the prevailing hippie culture of the 1960s, which was preoccupied with issues like war, environment, advertising, big business, television, and global artificiality. "Ziggy was also a sharp move away from the hippie culture of the 1960s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

podcast.title: Deteriorated Relationship with Brian Eno (Late 1970s)
podcast.body: The collaborative tandem between David Bowie and Brian Eno was exhausted, and their personal relationship deteriorated during the complex creative and recording process of *Lodger*. This led to them eventually pursuing different paths. "la relación personal entre David Bowie y Brian Hennon queda un tanto deteriorada a nivel personal."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: David Bowie: La trilogía de Berlin 3

podcast.title: Developing Fashion Sense
podcast.body: Bowie was actively cultivating a daring and interesting fashion sense, moving away from the prevailing hippie aesthetic of long hair and jeans. "Bowie was also developing a very interesting and daring fashion sense."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

podcast.title: Disconnection from Berlin Inspiration
podcast.body: Although David Bowie would later buy a house in Berlin, he became completely disconnected from Berlin as a source of inspiration after the *Lodger* period, affecting his creative direction. "quedaría completamente desconectado de Berling. No tanto físicamente, sino también en base a su inspiración, se desconectó totalmente de Berling."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: David Bowie: La trilogía de Berlin 3

podcast.title: Dismantling Pop Persona (Late 80s-Early 90s)
podcast.body: Following his ambivalence about mid-80s pop success, Bowie actively sought to dismantle his pop persona and reclaim his status as an "art pop avatar," pioneering alternative rock before the genre was formally named. "So, through the late 80s and early 90s, Bowie would seek to dismantle his pop persona and reclaim his status as an art pop avatar."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Drug-Induced Photography for Inspiration
podcast.body: In his drug-addled state in 1976, Bowie took up photography, despite not being particularly skilled at it. He would photograph anything he encountered on the street while completely intoxicated, using these images as raw inspiration for the strange paintings he was creating. "hacia fotografías totalmente drogado todo lo que se encontraba por la calle para lo intentarlo solo de inspiración para esos cuadros extraños que pintaba."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Pedro y el lobo de David Bowie

podcast.title: EMI Records Deal - $17.5 Million
podcast.body: In the 1980s, Bowie signed a new record deal with EMI Records worth $17.5 million, one of the biggest deals in the music industry at that time. This substantial contract influenced his decision to create a more commercially oriented album like "Let's Dance." "And then there was the new 17.5 million dollar record deal with EMI Records, one of the biggest deals in the industry to that time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early 70s Album Output
podcast.body: From the release of "Hunky Dory," Bowie was exceptionally prolific, releasing 11 studio albums and two live albums in just over eight and a half years, in addition to collaborations with other artists like Iggy Pop. "he had released 11 studio albums in just over 8 and a half years, plus two live albums."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Admiration for The Stooges
podcast.body: In the early 1970s, David Bowie expressed admiration for The Stooges as a band, even before he became a major star himself. "And if you were to go back to the early early 70s and ask a then new artist named David Bowie about the band's hemost admire, he'd say the stooges."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

podcast.title: Early Career Impact - The Most Discussed Rock Star
podcast.body: For over 40 years of his six-decade career, David Bowie was recognized as the most discussed, photographed, imitated, worshiped, and admired rock star in history. No other rock and roll performer had a more profound effect on music, with much of today's alt rock tracing its roots directly or indirectly to his work. "He was the most discussed, photographed, imitated, worshiped, and admired rock star in history."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Career Struggles as David Jones
podcast.body: Before adopting the name Bowie, David Jones was a saxophone player inspired by Little Richard and American R&B. He was in several unsuccessful bands and struggled to find a style that suited him throughout the 1960s. "Bowie, or David Jones, as he was known back then, which is his real name, tried really, really hard to make something happen with music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Career Struggles as David Jones
podcast.body: Before adopting his famous stage name, David Bowie was known by his birth name, David Jones. He began his musical career under this name and initially struggled to make an impact. "It was pretty, you know, spacious Bowie or David Jones as he was known back then, which is his real name, tried real hard to make something happen with music."

podcast.title: Early Career and Personal Struggles
podcast.body: Before his breakthrough, Bowie was a lost, wandering artist, taking mime lessons, and had recorded a series of albums that largely went nowhere. He was reduced to working for a company that made copies of legal documents for law firms. During this period, he endured a painful breakup with Hermione Farthingdale, which led to depression, feelings of loss, and a short dalliance with heroin. "Bowie had just endured a painful breakup with a woman named Hermione Farthingdale."

podcast.title: Early Internet Adoption
podcast.body: Bowie became interested in the internet around 1996-1997, realizing it would change everything, including music, long before it was mainstream. He had been using email since the late 1980s, before the public internet was widely available. He prophetically described the internet in a 1999 BBC interview as an "alien life form" that would establish "total fragmentation" and crush existing ideas of media through the interplay between users and providers. "No, it's an alien life form."

podcast.title: Iconic Haircut and Stylists
podcast.body: Bowie's new haircut was revolutionary and as historically significant as Elvis's curls or The Beatles' mop tops. Inspired by a model in a magazine wearing designs by Japanese fashion figure Kansai Yamamoto, the cut was replicated on Bowie by stylist Susie Fussy (his mom's hairdresser). It featured razor-cut sides and back, backcombed into a puffy fluff ball, and dyed a bright reddish-orange, transforming him into the "Elfin Cute Boy in the Dress." "Bowie's new haircut was every bit as important to rock history as Elvis's curls or the Beatles mop tops."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Image Changes and Public Imagination
podcast.body: Throughout his career, Bowie made a series of daring image changes that consistently captivated the public's imagination, marking distinct phases of his artistic journey. "He'd made a series of daring image changes, all of which captured the public's imagination."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Immense Influence (50-Year Career)
podcast.body: Bowie's death marked the close of an era, as few individuals have matched his influence over a career spanning approximately 50 years. His impact extended across music, fashion, and art, with much of his work remaining timeless. "Few people have been as influential as he'd been over the course of a career that extended about 50 years. That influence included music, fashion, and art."

podcast.title: Immense Influence on New Rock
podcast.body: David Bowie is considered uniquely influential in the world of New Rock, with his work in the 1970s being traceable as a root for genres like punk, new wave, industrial, and electronic music. His influence is evident in the sound and vision of numerous bands including Nirvana, the Sex Pistols, Foo Fighters, Nine Inch Nails, R.E.M., Smashing Pumpkins, The Killers, Scott Weiland, and Coldplay. He is described as "the Beatles of the alt rock set." "Take any genre of rock you like punk, new wave, industrial electronic and somehow you'll be able to trace it back to something that David Bowie did in the 1970s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Impact of Death
podcast.body: David Bowie's passing was highlighted as an example of how deeply fans are affected by the death of a musician, feeling a personal loss for someone they only knew through their art. "We saw it when Bowie died."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Importance for Gay People
podcast.body: David Bowie was one of the most significant figures for gay people in pop culture, having tremendous social and political implications, especially in the UK. His public statements and gender-bending image provided representation and courage to many marginalized individuals. "David Bowie was one of the most important figures for gay people that pop culture has ever seen."

podcast.title: Incalculable Impact of Ziggy Stardust
podcast.body: The impact of Bowie's Ziggy Stardust persona on rock music is considered "almost incalculable." In 1972, rock was dominated by jeans, t-shirts, and long hair, but Ziggy's makeup, costumes, and hair completely revolutionized the visual aspect of rock. "Now take it from me, the impact of Bowie's Ziggy Stardust on rock is almost incalculable, and here's why."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Incalculable Impact of Ziggy Stardust
podcast.body: Bowie's Ziggy Stardust character offered significant hope to many, presenting himself as a weirdly androgynous, potentially bisexual figure who wore makeup and glitter and performed provocative acts on stage, such as simulating oral sex with his guitarist, Mick Ronson. Despite Bowie himself not being 100% gay, the character's persona profoundly impacted and inspired closeted people worldwide. "Ziggy was this weirdly androgynous, maybe bisexual creature who wore makeup and glitter and did all kinds of looed things on stage, like simulating oral sex in his guitarist, Mick Ronson."

podcast.title: Indifference to Peter and the Wolf Release
podcast.body: When approached about the release of his *Peter and the Wolf* narration, David Bowie, who was by then in a post-rehabilitation state and embarking on a more "normal" creative phase (like the *Low* era), displayed complete indifference. He reportedly "didn't care in the slightest" about the album's fate. "a David Bogud que ya estaba por dentro de la interabilitario que en pleno ojo de la tecnología de Lorenzo había sido un personaje normal a la llave de guantos de Dios no lo importó lo más mínimo."

podcast.title: Influence of Vince Taylor
podcast.body: Bowie was inspired by Vince Taylor, an English-American singer who, following a mental crisis, believed himself to be an entity between a god and an alien, contributing to Ziggy's otherworldly aspect. "He'd also discovered Vince Taylor, an English American singer, with some kind of mental crisis and now believed that he existed somewhere between a god and an alien."

podcast.title: Influence on 21st Century Pop
podcast.body: Even during his absence from touring and new albums, David Bowie was widely cited as an influence and inspiration by a new generation of "chameleonic" pop artists, including Daft Punk, Lady Gaga, and Janelle Monáe, indicating his enduring impact on 21st-century music. "Even as he stopped releasing new albums or touring, David Bowie was being cited as an influence and inspiration by a new generation of pop-ats with chameleonic material, including daft punk. Lady Gaga. And Janelle Monet."

podcast.title: Influence on Blitz Kids and New Romantics
podcast.body: David Bowie was highly admired by the Blitz kids, who appreciated his ever-changing sense of style, use of makeup, and gender-bending presentation. His willingness to push boundaries provided a blueprint for their desire for glamour and non-conformity. "And Bowie, in his ever-changing sense of style, and makeup, and drudgedy, gender bending, fantastic for both boys and girls. David Bowie was the most appreciative of what the Blitz kids were trying to do."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on British Punk - Sex Pistols Connection
podcast.body: Bowie's "outsider-ness," short, sharp songs, wild fashion sense, and defiant attitude endeared him to alienated working-class youth who would become the first generation of British punks. His friendships with Iggy Pop and Lou Reed (of The Velvet Underground) also made him "cool" in their eyes. Famously, on July 2nd, 1973, after Bowie's final Ziggy Stardust tour show at the Hammersmith Odeon, a young Steve Jones (later guitarist for the Sex Pistols) stole microphones and amps from the venue, gear that would be used to start his new band. "A young thief named Steve Jones somehow got inside and helped himself to whatever he could carry out, mostly some microphones and some amps."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Jordan Mooney
podcast.body: Jordan Mooney, a key figure in British punk fashion, was described as a "big Bowie fan." Her early rebellious red and pink haircut, which led to her being kicked out of school, was an expression of this admiration. "When she was kicked out of school for her red and pink haircut, she was a big bowie fan."

The first generation of British punks admired his short, sharp songs, wild fashion sense, and defiant attitude. "David Bowie's outsider-ness of the early 1970s endeared him to other people who felt alienated and marginalized."

podcast.title: Influential Rock Artist
podcast.body: David Bowie is widely considered one of the most influential artists in the history of rock, with many musical paths tracing back to his work. His importance has grown even more significantly since his passing. "The more you study the history of rock, the more you realize just how many roads lead back to Bowie in some way or another."

podcast.title: Initial Reaction to Death
podcast.body: Upon hearing the news of his death, many initially believed it to be an internet hoax, given Bowie's special status and the fact he had just released a new album three days prior. The disbelief stemmed from his recent musical activity and perceived invincibility. "My initial reaction was this surely was another internet hoax. This was Bowie. He was special, probably immortal."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Inspiration for "Aladdin Sane" Name
podcast.body: The name for Bowie's new persona, "Aladdin Sane," was a phonetic play on "A Lad Insane," offering a glimpse into his mental state after the intense "Ziggy" experience and his concerns for his half-brother, Terry, who suffered from severe mental health issues. "He called his new image a Latin scene. Separate that to a lad in scene and you'll get the tiniest idea of where his head was at."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Inspiration for "Bowie" Name
podcast.body: David Jones chose the name "Bowie" after becoming somewhat obsessed with the character Jim Bowie, played by actor Richard Widmark in the movie "The Alamo." Jim Bowie was a real-life American pioneer, soldier, smuggler, and slave trader famous during the Battle of the Alamo in Texas. "Our David Jones had just seen a movie called The Alamo. He became somewhat obsessed with the character played by actor Richard Widmark. That character's name was Jim Bowie."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Inspiration for "Space Oddity" - Stanley Kubrick & Garden Gnomes
podcast.body: Bowie was heavily influenced by Stanley Kubrick's "2001, A Space Odyssey," which he saw while "stoned out of his mind" in 1968, leading to the creation of "Space Oddity." The character name "Major Tom" might also have been inspired by Tom Major, the father of future British Prime Minister John Major, who had a second career making garden gnomes. "But it's possible that the name of the character in the song was inspired by the story of a failed British trapezoid artist named Tom Major."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Inspiration for Dark Music
podcast.body: David Bowie was identified as one of the artists whose dark music attracted punk refugees, influencing the nascent Goth scene. "That would include David Bowie and joint-evision, the first version of Ultravox, and an Irish performance art group called The Virgin Proons."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Inspiration for LGBTQ+ Individuals
podcast.body: Bowie's public comments about his sexuality in 1972 struck a chord with thousands who were afraid to come out, giving them courage and a sense of shared identity with a famous figure. Figures like Boy George of Culture Club and Holly Johnson of Frankie Goes to Hollywood have stated that Bowie's comments changed their lives. "Bowie gave them the courage to be who they were."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Inspiration for Ziggy Stardust
podcast.body: David Bowie's iconic Ziggy Stardust character was partly inspired by Iggy Pop's persona, influencing the choice of the name "Ziggy." "That character was to be in part inspired by Iggy. I mean, why do you think Bowie chose the name Ziggy?"

podcast.body: Ziggy Stardust's costumes drew inspiration from the main characters of Stanley Kubrick's controversial film *A Clockwork Orange*, which was banned in the UK for its depictions of violence and sex, as well as from Japanese designer Yasuko Hayashi. "Ziggy's clothes were inspired in equal parts by what we saw with the main characters in the film, a clockwork orange... And a Japanese designer named Yasuko Hayashi."

podcast.body: Bowie was significantly inspired by Marc Bolan of T-Rex. Bolan's stage attitude, aesthetic, and musical compositions deeply influenced Bowie's work in the 1970s, making him a central figure of inspiration. "Siempre se recuerda como la persona que inspiraba David Bowie."

podcast.title: Ironic Quotation Marks for "Heroes"
podcast.body: David Bowie treated the song and album "Heroes" with detachment, intentionally putting ironic quotation marks around the title. This "arch gesture" meant both the song and the album were officially called, "quote, heroes, unquote," even though the song is now unironically beloved and recognized as a global anthem. podcast.title: Kanye West Prediction Theory
podcast.body: A conspiracy theory claims David Bowie predicted the rise of Kanye West back in 1972. Proponents cite Bowie's *Ziggy Stardust and the Spiders from Mars* album (released June 16, 1972) and its song "Five Years" as foretelling the event, noting Kanye's birth on June 8, 1977, almost five years later. The theory also highlights the "K. West" sign visible on the *Ziggy Stardust* album cover (from a fur store), interpreting it as a direct reference, and Bowie's final album, *Black Star*, as an "anointment" of Kanye, referred to as a "Black Star." Bowie's known visionary capabilities regarding digital music, social media, and gender fluidity are used to support his ability to predict Kanye's ascendance. "Did David Bowie predict the rise of Kanye West way back in 1972?"

podcast.body: Bowie's three albums created in Berlin with Brian Eno were explicitly "Kraftwerk inspired." "He created three craftwork inspired albums with producer Brian Eno that show that maybe electronics were the way for."

podcast.title: Krautrock and Berlin Influence
podcast.body: David Bowie was profoundly "shaken and inspired" by early Krautrock, especially Kraftwerk, which led him to move to Berlin. This period resulted in three of his most fascinating albums: "Low," "Heroes," and "Lodger," with the B-side of the "Heroes" single, "V-2 Schneider," directly named after Florian Schneider. "David Bowie was so shaken and inspired by early crop rock and craftwork in particular, as he moved to Berlin and made three of his most fascinating albums as a result."

podcast.title: Lack of Formal Musical Training
podcast.body: Bowie did not possess formal musical training, unlike many of his contemporaries. This was viewed as a positive attribute, as it allowed him to avoid the constraints of conventional musical "rules." "Sometimes it helps to not be constrained by what you think the rules are."

podcast.title: Late 1980s Creative Reassessment
podcast.body: After facing disappointment with albums like "Tonight" (1984) and "Never Let Me Down" (1987), Bowie decided to "switch gears again" in 1988, recognizing that hard rock would move away from hair metal towards a more primal sound. He aimed to make music he personally enjoyed, rather than chasing audience preferences. "So Bowie decided to switch gears again. In 1988, he saw how the way the wind was blowing. Heavy and hard rock was going to move away from hair metal and into something more primal over the next few years. Bowie was into this music at the time and wanted to pursue this sound. Instead of chasing what audiences wanted, he was once again to make music that he liked."

podcast.title: Late Touring Career Rider – Minimalist Demands
podcast.body: In the late stages of his touring career, David Bowie became remarkably undemanding. His rider simply asked for a fruit bowl and that his dressing room be maintained at a specific temperature, between 14 and 18 degrees Celsius. "All he asked for was a fruit bowl and that he required his dressing room to be kept at a temperature between 14 and 18 degrees Celsius."

podcast.body: In 1985, Bowie again came to Iggy Pop's aid by listening to rough tapes of new songs and encouraging Iggy and Steve Jones to make another album, leading to "Blah Blah Blah." "In 1985, it was Bowie to the Rescue again. After listening to some rough tapes of some new songs, he encouraged Iggy and his new buddy, ex-sex pistol guitar Steve Jones, to make another album."

podcast.title: Leading Visionary of Rock (Late 1970s)
podcast.body: As the 1970s drew to a close, Bowie was widely regarded as the leading visionary in rock music. He was consistently several steps ahead of his contemporaries, possessing acute instincts for future trends, or perhaps, actively shaping the direction in which he wanted music to evolve. "He was always several steps ahead of everybody else. And his instincts for what was to come next were bang on."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Liberating Aesthetic Against Stereotypes
podcast.body: He is considered an icon of culture who promoted a philosophy where "what you are doesn't matter, but what you feel and what makes you happy, and that you don't have to name things." This informed much of his aesthetic, which was very liberating, allowing men for the first time to dress like women, not be masculine, or not fit into existing stereotypes without being linked to specific sexual orientations. He was a great step forward against sexual stereotypes. "Que la llevó muchísimo a toda su estética y que fue una estética muy liberadora, porque por primera vez podíamos tener hombres que se desquien con mujeres o que no querían ser masculinos o que no querían encajar dentro de estos estereotipos y no por ello tenían que estar vinculados a unas opciones sexuales o a otras."

podcast.body: In the summer of 2014, Bowie began feeling unwell and was diagnosed with liver cancer, which was initially treatable. podcast.body: David Bowie battled liver cancer for 18 months before succumbing to the disease. He passed away on a Sunday afternoon in January 2016, after fighting the illness for a considerable period. "David Boyle was taken away from us by liver cancer."

"The gap following the release of Bowie's scary monsters was the longest gap between albums in his career, a little more than two and a half years."

podcast.title: Longest Album Gap and RCA Departure (Early 1980s)
podcast.body: Bowie experienced the longest gap in his career to date—three years—before releasing a new studio album, largely due to his unhappiness with RCA Records and his efforts to get out of his contract, driven by a desire to try new things and pursue a new sound. "It would be another three years before Bowie returned with a new studio album, the longest gap in his career to date."

podcast.title: Los Angeles Cocaine Psychosis (1970s) – Station to Station Blackout
podcast.body: During his mid-1970s Los Angeles period, David Bowie survived almost exclusively on milk, red peppers, and cocaine, which induced extreme paranoia. podcast.title: Move to Berlin - Cold War Artistic Hub
podcast.body: In an effort to escape the negative influences surrounding him in L.A. and kick his cocaine addiction, Bowie and Iggy Pop moved to Berlin, Germany. During the height of the Cold War, Berlin was a divided city, yet its unique artistic and bohemian culture provided the perfect environment for Bowie's musical evolution, where he immersed himself in German electronic and crude rock sounds. "He and Iggy Pop packed up and left for Berlin. Now Berlin. Nobody went to Berlin. This was the height of the Cold War."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Move to West Berlin with Iggy Pop
podcast.body: Deeply influenced by German electronic groups like Kraftwerk, Can, and Neu!, and envisioning electronic music as the future, Bowie moved to West Berlin with Iggy Pop to immerse themselves in the local scene and simultaneously recover from their addictions. They settled in a modest place at Hopstresser 155 in the Schöneberg area, motivated by a belief that remaining in Los Angeles would lead to their demise. "He began to think that these electronic methods of producing music were the future. And what better way to follow this muse than to move to where it all seemed to be happening? Germany."

podcast.title: New Romantic Scene Influence

His artistic direction provided a significant musical blueprint for the burgeoning movement. "The sound of his 1979 album, Lager, and especially his 1980 records, Scary Monsters and Super Creeps, were massive influences on the young New Romantics."

podcast.title: New Wave Pioneer Status

podcast.title: New York City Residence
podcast.body: After his 2004 heart attack, Bowie lived a reclusive life in a luxurious penthouse at 285 Lafayette Street in New York City's Soho Nolita area. The 5,100-square-foot residence featured direct elevator access, 11-foot ceilings, a large library, four bedrooms, four bathrooms, and three terraces. He occasionally went out, sometimes with his wife and daughter, and enjoyed Washington Square Park. He used disguises like sunglasses, a hat, and carrying a Greek language newspaper to deter recognition. "As you might expect, it was a lovely place, filled with fine, expensive art, tastefully decorated, and with an interior crafted by architects and designers from Europe."

podcast.title: Numerous Honors and Legacy
podcast.body: Bowie is enshrined in the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, the Songwriter's Hall of Fame, and the Science Fiction and Fantasy Hall of Fame. The BBC once named him the best-dressed Briton in history. A species of spider, an asteroid (342843 David Bowie), and British postal stamps have been named in his honor. A statue of him stands in Ailsbury, UK, where he first introduced Ziggy Stardust, and a street in Paris bears his name. "I think I could go on, but I probably have made my point."

podcast.title: Obsession with Hitler and Nazi Sympathies (Mid-1970s)
podcast.body: Bowie developed a dangerous obsession with Hitler and the Third Reich during his drug-addled period, frequently discussing Nazis in interviews. In 1976, he controversially told Playboy magazine that Hitler was one of the first rock stars, and was seen giving what appeared to be a Nazi salute to a crowd at a London train station. "And if that wasn't enough, Bowie had become obsessed with Hitler and the Third Reich."

"One version of the story says that during the sessions for what would become the Ziggy Stardust and the spiders from Mars album, Bowie woke up one morning and said to Angie over his orange juice, I want to cut my hair and I want to look different."

podcast.title: Patronage of Iggy Pop and The Stooges
podcast.body: Bowie was a great admirer and musical hero of Iggy Pop, fascinated by his craziness, almost constant mental instability, and ability to see beyond the drugs and self-destructive stage antics to Iggy's intelligence. Bowie convinced his manager to take on Iggy and The Stooges as a project, providing a cash injection that funded their *Raw Power* album. He later visited Iggy when he was in a mental hospital. Bowie's acceptance of Iggy also helped propel the first three Stooges albums to become important templates for punk rock. "Iggy's craziness had made him into one of Bowie's musical heroes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Patronage of Lou Reed
podcast.body: Bowie was also a great admirer of Lou Reed and The Velvet Underground, recognizing Reed's talent despite him being on the fringes and largely unknown. Bowie offered his patronage, leading him to produce Reed's 1972 album *Transformer*, collaborating with his Spiders From Mars guitarist, Mick Ronson, to help Reed find a new sound. "Bowie did, though, and he offered to lend his patronage to Lou."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Paving the Way for LGBTQ+ Artists
podcast.body: David Bowie's public persona and actions demonstrated that artists could identify as gay, bisexual, or at least sexually ambiguous and still thrive in the rock world. His influence encouraged more musicians to adopt similar approaches over the subsequent decade, contributing significantly to the rock community's gradual "climb out of the closet."

podcast.title: Personal Impact of Terry's Mental Health
podcast.body: The "Ziggy" experience was incredibly intense for all involved, and Bowie was also deeply affected by his adored half-brother, Terry, who suffered terribly from manic depression and schizophrenia and required hospitalization. Terry later died by suicide more than a decade later, by lying down in front of a train. "Not only had the Ziggy experience been crazy for all involved, but he also had a half brother. He adored named Terry, who was suffering terribly with mental health issues."

podcast.title: Personal Struggles (Mid-1970s)
podcast.body: Despite his global superstardom, Bowie was in a terrible personal state in the mid-1970s. He was drinking heavily and had developed a powerful cocaine addiction, leading him to believe he was "going quite insane" and worrying about witches and UFOs. Paradoxically, these struggles did not diminish his influence, but rather made him appear even more mysterious and, consequently, bigger. "He was going quite insane, worried about witches and UFOs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Personal Struggles with Fame and Substance Abuse
podcast.body: Despite his immense success, Bowie's personal life in the mid-1970s was fraught with heavy drinking and a powerful cocaine addiction. He also experienced paranoia, worrying about witches and UFOs, which contributed to his increasing mysteriousness and public allure. "But personally Bowie was in terrible shape. He was drinking a lot and it developed a powerful appetite for cocaine and he was going a little insane too."

podcast.title: Physical Vinyl Artwork of Black Star
podcast.body: The physical vinyl edition of Black Star is considered an artwork in itself, designed by a "great talent" in physical musical production. It hides secrets, such as reacting to ultraviolet rays and revealing a starry sky when exposed to sunlight, with the possibility of more undiscovered details. "el vinilo como pieza física también es una auténtica obra de arte en el igual que el disco porque nos deja un montón de secretos que hemos ido descubriendo lo largo de estos meses y de este año, sabemos que reacciona los rayos otra violeta, también sabemos que si lo pones a la luz del sol les aloncile estrellado y posiblemente nos quede algún detalle más por descubrir el largo de este tiempo."

podcast.title: Pioneer of Digital Distribution
podcast.body: David Bowie demonstrated foresight regarding the digital future of music by releasing his "Hours" album on September 21st, 1999, making it the first album by a major artist legally available for online download two weeks before its physical release. "Some like David Bowie saw a digital future coming. On September 21st of 1999, he released his hours album, and it became the first album by a major artist available for legal online download."

podcast.title: Pioneer of Sexual Ambiguity and Gay Icon
podcast.body: Bowie was candid, whether truthful or not, about his sexual orientation, introducing sexual ambiguity into mainstream culture. In doing so, he became a powerful gay icon, opening doors for countless gay performers and helping to launch a gay activist element within rock and pop music. "He introduced sexual ambiguity into mainstream culture, and in doing so became a powerful gay icon, opening the doors for hundreds if not thousands of gay performers, thereby launching a gay activist element in rock and pop."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pioneering Online Presence
podcast.body: David Bowie was one of the very first artists to launch a website, demonstrating his early adoption and understanding of digital platforms long before they became commonplace for musicians. "He was also one of the very first artists to have a website."

podcast.title: Pop Success as a "Costume"
podcast.body: Bowie approached pop success as "one more cloak to try on and then discard," treating pop stardom like a costume. This contrasted with artists like Lou Reed or Joni Mitchell, who found that experimentation often led to commercial toxicity, while Bowie successfully experimented and scored hits before, during, and after his artistic explorations, setting a new template for shape-shifters with pop aspirations. "For Bowie, pop success was one more cloak to try on and then discard."

podcast.title: Post-"Let's Dance" Creative Struggles
podcast.body: The immense success of "Let's Dance" unexpectedly confused Bowie, making him feel detached from his audience and uncertain of their expectations. This "confused headspace" initiated a creative downturn for the rest of the 1980s, as his subsequent work was unfairly judged against the commercial peak of "Let's Dance." "I suddenly felt very apart from my audience and it was depressing because I didn't know what they wanted."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Aladdin Sane Era
podcast.body: After his Aladdin Sane persona, David Bowie transitioned away from glam to become a "decidedly non-glam blue-eyed soul singer" by 1976-1977. "Bowie had moved on from Aladdin's saying to a stint as a decidedly non-glam blue-eyed soul singer."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

podcast.title: Post-Berlin Trilogy Career Shift
podcast.body: Over three years, David Bowie cleaned himself up and achieved new artistic goals with the Berlin Trilogy, though he distanced himself from mainstream pop success. At the dawn of the 1980s, he began to make his way back onto the charts, aiming to fully re-enter the pop landscape on his own terms, a strategic pivot that would help define the next wave of New Wave music. "So, over the course of three years, Boey had cleaned himself up and achieved new artistic goals with the Berlin Trilogy, but divorced himself from pop success."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Post-Death World Deterioration
podcast.body: Many people observed a noticeable decline in global affairs after Bowie's death, leading to a "meme" that the world "kind of started going a hell" after he died. This includes political, social, economic, and technological shifts like Brexit, Putin's actions, the Ukraine conflict, COVID, Gaza, and the rise of AI. "I'm sure it's all a coincidence, but it's no exaggeration to say that since Bowie died, we've transitioned into a completely different world."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Heart Attack Seclusion and Subsequent Heart Attacks
podcast.body: The heart attack scare in 2004 prompted David Bowie to re-evaluate his life, leading him to live in seclusion for the remainder of his life. It is reported that he experienced at least another five heart attacks between 2004 and his death in 2016. "But that heart attack scare caused him to re-evaluate everything. He chose to live in seclusion for the rest of his life. And word is that he had at least another five heart attacks between 2004 and 2016."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Let's Dance Audience Alienation
podcast.body: Following the immense commercial success of "Let's Dance," Bowie felt a profound sense of alienation from his new audience, questioning their connection to his artistic roots. This psychological impact marked the beginning of a creative "spiral" that continued throughout the rest of the 1980s, as his subsequent work was often judged against his previous innovations. "I remember looking out over these waves of people who were coming to hear this record played live and thinking, I wonder how many velvet underground albums these people have in their record collections. I suddenly felt very apart from my audience, and it was depressing because I didn't know what they wanted."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Tin Machine Return to Solo Career
podcast.body: After Tin Machine broke up in 1992, David Bowie reverted to his solo identity, achieving "decent success," though not on the same scale as his iconic 1970s and early 1980s period. "After Tin Machine broke up in 1992, David Bowie went back to being, well, David Bowie. He had some decent success, but nothing like what we saw in the 70s and early 80s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Posthumous Critical Re-evaluation
podcast.body: The posthumous success of Black Star, reaching No. 1 on charts and receiving awards, significantly altered the perception of David Bowie's later career. Previously, albums like *Hitin*, *Hours*, and *Reality* had faced criticism regarding their musical quality, but Black Star's impact led to a re-evaluation, solidifying his final work as a significant artistic legacy. "Resulta triste que a David Bowie le añandado el número 1 en todas las listas y le añandado todos estos premios postumos cuando los últimos albumes de la carrera de David Bowie sobre todo los últimos tres, cuatro albumes, el hitin, el hours, el reality, habían sido un tanto cuestionado por su calidad musical."
