podcast.title: Professional Ballet Aspirations
podcast.body: While living in Geneva in 1976, Bowie aspired to become a professional ballet dancer. He brought a professional British dancer friend to Geneva, paying him substantial amounts for private dance lessons as he pursued this expensive endeavor. "bailar como venerin profesional y teníamos amigo que era el enlombra profesional británico a la se gastaba un montón de dinero y traerse lo de vio al cinebra y le pagaba un lote en tido dinerad por clase profesionales de danza."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Pedro y el lobo de David Bowie

podcast.title: Profound Influence
podcast.body: David Bowie is considered one of the most influential musicians ever, arguably influencing more musical genres than even The Beatles due to his constant reinvention. His artistic DNA can be found across glam, punk, art rock, folk, hard rock, grunge, industrial music, electronic music, indie rock, and hip-hop. He brought an unprecedented level of sophistication to rock music, and his work continues to be studied, finding new fans across generations. "His DNA can be found in glam, punk, art rock folk, hard rock, grunge, industrial music, electronic music of all flavors, indie rock, and hip-hop."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Program Introduction
podcast.body: David Bowie was mentioned as providing an introduction to a program about changes in music over the decades, setting the stage for discussions on music history and technological impacts. "David Bowie with an introduction to this program on changes in music over the decades."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Prolific Abstract Painting
podcast.body: During his 1976 esthetic phase, David Bowie became a prolific painter, producing thousands of abstract and "esthetic" pictures, often completing them in as little as five minutes. He painted continuously, creating a vast body of work, though the quality and complexity of these quickly produced pieces were not noted as exceptional. "pintaba de mayor composición miles de cuadros pero miles continuamente cuadros un poco abstractos y esténicos que le pintaban cinco minutos pero no paraba."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Pedro y el lobo de David Bowie

podcast.title: Prolific Output (1970s)
podcast.body: Bowie's rise to stardom was characterized by an incredible prolificness, releasing "album after album, single after single, character after character, tour after tour." This constant stream of new material was remarkable, especially as his records were commercial and critical successes and each was distinct from the last, creating immense mystery and public curiosity. "That prolificness was a big part of Bowie's rise to start him."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Prolific Output in the 70s/80s
podcast.body: From "Hunky Dory" onward, Bowie released 11 studio albums and two live albums in just over eight and a half years. During this intense period, he also collaborated with artists like Iggy Pop, survived a deep cocaine addiction, and expanded his artistic endeavors into film and theater, taking on projects that regular rock stars typically avoided. "I mean, after all, if we take Hunky Dory as the first album where Bowie got his groove, he had released 11 studio albums in just over 8 and a half years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Prophetic Musical Vision
podcast.body: Bowie possessed an unparalleled ability to "see 'round corners and predicted the future of rock," evolving through genres from folk to glam, blue-eyed soul, electronic, early industrial, and Technopop, demonstrating an extraordinary foresight in music trends. "Bowie saw round corners and predicted the future of rock unlike anyone we've ever seen."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Peaked Too Soon - Bands That Were Ahead of Their Time

podcast.title: Proto-New Wave Artist
podcast.body: David Bowie was considered a precursor to New Wave, embodying the genre's characteristics before the term became widespread, yet some American radio programmers who dismissed New Wave had no issue playing his music. "This is from the same people who had no trouble playing tons of David Bowie, a guy who was New Wave before there was such a thing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 1: New Wave

podcast.title: Public Cross-Dressing and Controversy (1970s)
podcast.body: By the 1970s, Bowie deliberately courted scandal by publicly wearing dresses and carrying a purse, challenging conventional gender presentation.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 9

podcast.title: Public Declaration of Sexuality
podcast.body: In January 1972, Bowie publicly professed to be gay in an interview in *Melody Maker* magazine. This statement was far more scandalous in 1970s Britain than his earlier cross-dressing, as homosexuality had only been decriminalized in the UK in 1967. This declaration made his previous dress-wearing seem "minuscule." "The big media storm came when Bowie publicly professed to be gay in an interview in Melody Maker magazine in January of 1972."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Public Perception of Immortality
podcast.body: Bowie was perceived as eternal and immortal, making the concept of a world without him unthinkable for many. "Bowie was supposed to be different, eternal, immortal. The world of rock without Bowie? Unthinkable."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 2: The Role of Indie Rock

podcast.title: Puffball Haircut as Creative Catalyst
podcast.body: Bowie's "puff ball" haircut transcended mere fashion, appearing to propel him onto an entirely new and exceptionally creative musical trajectory, which subsequently unleashed a wave of influence across all of rock and roll. "So there's Bowie and his puff ball, a hugely important haircut, not just in terms of style and fashion sense, but it seems to have sent Bowie down an entirely new ultra creative musical path, which in turn created a wave of influence that ended up affecting all rock and roll."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pushing for Better Sound
podcast.body: David Bowie was among the artists, including Yes and Supertramp, who placed great importance on achieving high-quality concert sound. Their insistence "pushed sound companies to get better," contributing to advancements in live audio technology and services. "But to performers like David Bowie and Yes and Super Tramp, getting concert sound right was very, very important, so they pushed sound companies to get better."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Randomness and Contrast in Music
podcast.body: From *Low* onward, Brian Eno taught Bowie that not all songs need to tell a story. Randomness and contrast became recurring characteristics in the careers of both artists. "Y no también le enseño que no todas las canciones tienen por qué contar una historia. A partir de ese disco, la leatoriedad del contraste serían características recurrentes para la carrera de ambos."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: El proyecto que salvó a David Bowie. La trilogía de Berlín

podcast.title: Recanting Sexuality Claims
podcast.body: Bowie later recanted his claims of being gay or even bisexual. This retraction led to significant criticism from gay rights activists, who felt he had withdrawn support from the community he initially inspired. "Bowie would later recant claims of being gay or even bisexual, something that resulted in plenty of criticism from the gay rights activists."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Recording of Peter and the Wolf
podcast.body: During his eccentric period in Switzerland, David Bowie recorded an orchestral version of Prokofiev's *Peter and the Wolf*, with himself narrating the story. This project illustrates his "un poco falla" (a bit off) mental state at the time. "La paranoia está que hizo David Bowie sobre Pedro y el obo de Procofir, en el cual grabó a un orquesto tocando Pedro y el obo y él se grababa narrando el cuento de Pedro y el obo, es justo de esta época."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: David Bowie: La trilogía de Berlin 1

podcast.title: Relationship with Mick Jagger
podcast.body: In the early 1970s, David Bowie and Mick Jagger, both known for sexual experimentation, became close friends after a 1973 Bowie concert. They were frequently seen together in public, including clubs, concerts, and even at a Muhammad Ali fight, with one biographer crediting Bowie for introducing Jagger to gay culture. Bowie's backup singer, Aiba Cherry, claimed the two were "sexually obsessed with each other" and she witnessed them having sex, with associates confirming their close relationship during which they "practically lived together for several months." David's ex-wife, Angela Bowie, claimed on the Joan Rivers show in 1990 that she caught them naked and asleep in bed together. "Mick and Dave were really sexually obsessed with each other. Even though I was in bed with them many times, I ended up just watching them have sex. They became very close and practically lived together for several months."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Relocation to Berlin with Iggy Pop
podcast.body: After Iggy Pop's hospitalization, David Bowie and Iggy moved to Berlin, where they both cleaned up their drug habits and successfully restarted their respective careers. "Iggy and Bowie moved to Berlin, cleaned up and restarted their careers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

podcast.title: Richie Edwards' Musical Influence
podcast.body: David Bowie was a significant musical influence on Richie Edwards of the Manic Street Preachers, among other artists. "He was into the Smiths and David Bowie."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Uncharted "Sneak Peak" - Episode 9: The Disappearance of Richey Edwards

podcast.title: Robotic Electronic Experiments
podcast.body: Some of David Bowie's electronic experiments exhibited a similar robotic, cold, artificial, emotionally sterile, and intense vibe to early Technopop artists like Kraftwerk and The Normal. This aesthetic characterized a significant portion of the emerging electronic music scene. "That description can also be applied to craft work, the normal and some of Bowie's electronic experiments."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rock Legend Comparison - Less Flashy than Bowie
podcast.body: Christine McVie is mentioned in comparison to David Bowie, highlighting that she was not as flashy as Bowie or Prince. This comparison emphasizes McVie's self-effacing and shy nature contrasting with more flamboyant rock legends. "Someone not as flashy as Prince or David Bowie."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Role in Fall of Berlin Wall
podcast.body: The German Federal Foreign Office publicly thanked Bowie for his role in the eventual fall of the Berlin Wall, acknowledging his cultural impact beyond music. "When he died, the German federal foreign office thanked Bowie for his role in the eventual fall of the Berlin Wall."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Sales and Enduring Cult Status
podcast.body: Throughout his career, Bowie sold over 140 million records worldwide. Beyond commercial success, he cultivated one of the biggest and most enduring cults in the history of music, driven by his unique artistry and image control. "The entire time he made music that not only sold 140 million plus records, but also created one of the biggest and most enduring cults in the history of music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Saved by the American Space Program
podcast.body: The American space program is credited with diverting Bowie from a potential life of photocopying and mime, setting him up to become one of the most important artists of the 1970s. "But the thing that saved Bowie from a life of photocopying in mime abuse was the American space program."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Savior of Iggy Pop's Career
podcast.body: Bowie visited Iggy Pop in a psychiatric hospital when no one else cared, convincing him not to kill himself and subsequently securing him a new management deal and record contract. This intervention was crucial for Iggy's professional and personal survival. "Bowie was the only person in the world who cared about what happened to Iggy Pop and it was him who finally convinced Iggy that he didn't need to kill himself."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About Iggy Pop

podcast.title: Savior of The Stooges
podcast.body: Leveraging his influence and industry power, David Bowie convinced Iggy Pop and the Ashton brothers, along with James Williamson, to move to England to record the *Raw Power* album for Columbia Records, effectively restarting The Stooges' career. "Bowie, although not in the greatest shape himself when it came to drugs, turned out to be Iggy's and ultimately the studio's savior."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

podcast.title: Saxophone Teacher
podcast.body: The saxophone part on Lou Reed's "Walk on the Wild Side" was played by the individual who taught David Bowie how to play the sax when Bowie was about 14 years old, showcasing an interesting connection in their musical history. "The saxophone part was played by the guy who taught Bowie how to play the sax when he was about 14."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Book of World Records Version 1.0 - Part 2

podcast.title: Scarcity of Information on Black Star
podcast.body: The details surrounding Black Star's creation are sparse, largely due to David Bowie's death just three days after its release, his reclusive nature in his final period, and the fact that most collaborators were unaware of his terminal illness, limiting shared information. "la muerte de David Bowie fue tres días después de su lanzamiento, Tony Bizkonti tampoco nos dice mucho, fue una etapa en la que le estaba bastante recluido, no compartía mucha información."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Secret Messages in Music (early-mid 1970s)
podcast.body: Bowie was convinced he was trying to send secret messages to himself through his music. To uncover these, he had a special turntable custom-made, which allowed him to listen to his own records played backwards. "He had a special turntable made so we could listen to his own records backwards because Bowie was convinced he was sending secret messages to himself."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Secret Recording of "The Next Day"
podcast.body: Bowie managed to record his album "The Next Day" in complete secrecy over two years in the internet age, a feat considered miraculous. This was achieved through the unwavering loyalty of his associates, who were sworn to secrecy, and by Bowie living a remarkably low-key life in New York City with Iman. He was often seen walking, grocery shopping, and attending social events, but people were accustomed to his flamboyant personas and simply didn't notice "David Jones." "How could one of the most famous musicians in the history of the universe manage to record an album in total secrecy in the age of the internet? It was a miracle."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Semi-Obscure Songs Covered on MTV Unplugged
podcast.body: Both Stone Temple Pilots and Nirvana chose to perform "semi obscure songs by David Bowie" as part of their MTV Unplugged sets, highlighting a shared artistic appreciation between the bands and the influential artist. "both STP and Nirvana chose to cover semi obscure songs by David Bowie as part of their sets."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Shape-Shifting Persona and Identity
podcast.body: Bowie embraced being different offstage from his onstage personas, unlike many rock artists who strive for authenticity. He curated characters like Ziggy Stardust, Aladdin Sane, Halloween Jack, the plastic soul man, and the Thin White Duke, frequently changing his image and character to capture public imagination and drive his artistic evolution. "It's very hard to convince people that you can be quite different offstage in rock and more than you are onstage."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Shared Flat in Berlin
podcast.body: After recording *The Idiot* (Iggy Pop's first solo album), David Bowie and Iggy Pop found and shared a modest flat in Berlin. "han encontrado en un modesto piso en Berlin, el cual compartieron."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: El proyecto que salvó a David Bowie. La trilogía de Berlín

podcast.title: Showman Persona
podcast.body: Even during his most artistic period, David Bowie embraced his role as a showman, as demonstrated by the creation of the "Peace on Earth" section in his duet with Bing Crosby, specifically designed to highlight his counterpoint vocals. "Even in the midst of his most arty period, David Boey could not resist the opportunity to be a showman."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Sound + Vision Tour - Retiring Hits
podcast.body: To shed the "baggage" of his past successes and start fresh, Bowie undertook the Sound + Vision Tour, during which he promised to play his old hits like "Space Oddity," "Ziggy Stardust," "Rebel Rebel," "Young Americans," "Heroes," and "Let's Dance" one last time before retiring them forever. His intention was to clear the decks and move forward creatively. "The first was something called the Sound Invision Tour where Bowie promised to play his old hits one more time and then retire them forever."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Spider Species
podcast.body: A spider species, *headropodid David Bowie*, has been named after David Bowie. This spider is found in Malaysia and is characterized by being large, yellow, and hairy. "Lusefran David Bowie has his own spider, headropodid David Bowie, which lives in Malaysia."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Spokesman for International League for the Preservation of Animal Filaments
podcast.body: In the early 1960s, before achieving widespread fame, David Bowie (then David Jones) acted as a spokesman for a group called the International League for the Preservation of Animal Filaments, advocating for men's right to wear long hair. "In the early 1960s, long before anybody knew who he was, Bowie was a spokesman for a group called the International League for the Preservation of Animal Filaments."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Spokesman for International League for the Preservation of Animal Filaments
podcast.body: In November 1964, David Jones appeared on a BBC News program as the founder, president, and spokesman for this organization. Its purpose was to advocate for the social acceptance of young British men wearing long hair. "The first time anyone really heard about him was when he appeared on a BBC News program in November of 1964 as the founder, president, and spokesman for the International League for the Preservation of Animal Filaments."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Stolen Microphones Used by Sex Pistols
podcast.body: During a Ziggy Stardust performance in London, thugs broke in after the show and stole all the band's microphones. One of these thieves was Steve Jones, who subsequently used those very microphones in his new band, the Sex Pistols. "One of those thieves was a kid named Steve Jones, and those mics were literally used in his new band called the Sex Pistols."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Strategic Catalog Lease During Internet Upheaval
podcast.body: Bowie leased his catalog for a 10-year period just before the internet "nearly destroyed the recorded music industry." This strategic timing allowed him to avoid financial losses from music piracy and declining CD sales, collecting a payday of $55 million. At the end of the term, he regained ownership and began earning money through streaming, owning everything by his death in 2016. "What's even more remarkable was his timing. He leased his catalog for a period of 10 years just before the internet nearly destroyed the recorded music industry. And while everyone else was losing money because of music piracy and dropping CD sales, Roy laughed all the way to the bank with a payday of $55 million."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Peaked Too Soon - Bands That Were Ahead of Their Time

podcast.title: Struggling for Image and Sound (Late 1960s)
podcast.body: Around the time The Velvet Underground, The Stooges, MC5, and Captain Beefheart were making records, David Bowie was struggling to define his own image, style, and sound, without much success. "Well, he was trying to find himself. He was trying to come up with an image and a style and a sound that would work for him and he wasn't doing very well."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Successful Publicity Stunt
podcast.body: Bowie's "gay confession," though later implied to be untrue, was a calculated publicity stunt designed to generate headlines. Far from damaging his career, this "simple, albeit untrue, statement" paradoxically enhanced his mystique and boosted his popularity.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 9

podcast.title: Suede Influence
podcast.body: David Bowie was celebrated by Suede as an influence, representing the great eccentric English rock of the 1970s and 1980s that Suede sought to revive. "Instead, Swade celebrated the great eccentric English rock of the 70s and 80s. David Bowie, Roxy Music, T-Rex, Smiths, Morrissey, British Psych, Jagger Swagger, Glam guitars..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Support and Production for Lou Reed
podcast.body: David Bowie was a devoted fan of the Velvet Underground and became a crucial figure in Lou Reed's solo career. He provided financial support for Lou Reed's second solo album, "Transformer," and co-produced it alongside his guitarist, Mick Ronson. Bowie's involvement was pivotal in launching Lou Reed's solo career, despite the controversial nature of the album's themes. "David Bowie era un gran fanático de la Belbet Underground."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Tras los pasos de Lou Reed

podcast.title: Support and Production for Lou Reed
podcast.body: By 1975, Bowie was a "genuine international superstar" whose patronage was instrumental in Lou Reed's solo career. "Thanks largely to the patronage of David Bowie, who by 1975 was a genuine international superstar."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Support for Lou Reed
podcast.body: By 1975, Bowie was a "genuine international superstar" whose patronage was instrumental in Lou Reed's solo career. "Thanks largely to the patronage of David Bowie, who by 1975 was a genuine international superstar."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Susie Fussy - Hairdresser for Ziggy Stardust
podcast.body: Susie Fussy, a London hairdresser, was instrumental in bringing Ziggy Stardust's look to life; she received the Vogue magazine inspiration from Bowie and Angie, then executed the distinctive cut and dyed it a reddish-orange hue for dramatic effect. "And they took the magazine and showed it to a London hairdresser named Susie Fussy who then gave Bowie the cut and died at that reddish orange for added effect."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Swimming Pool Exorcism Belief (early-mid 1970s)
podcast.body: In the early to mid-1970s, Bowie became convinced that his swimming pool was possessed by Satan. He refused to immerse even a toe into the pool until an exorcism was performed. "He believed his swimming pool was possessed by Satan. He refused to dip so much as a toe into the pool until somebody performed an exorcism."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Swiss Residence and Obsessions
podcast.body: Around the time he seemed to be at his lowest point, David Bowie moved to a millionaire house by a lake in Switzerland, which offered him a "hermetismo" or sense of privacy. During this period, he developed intense obsessions with painting (creating several canvases daily, often unfinished), contemporary art (amassing one of the world's most important collections), photography, dance, and classical music, seeking out expensive teachers for these pursuits. "se muda a una casa millonaria en suiza. Es la etapa en la que además de David Bowie sufren auténtico expolio económico por algunas de las personas que les rodeaban, cambia varias veces de mana, ya se ven, en vuelto en varias trifulcas legales, con bastante gente, está casi prácticamente divorciado, ya vive separado."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: David Bowie: La trilogía de Berlin 1

podcast.title: Talent and Role in Glam History
podcast.body: David Bowie is acknowledged for his "great talent" and his role in bringing glam to its "golden age" in the early 1970s. However, the transcript also suggests that he might not have been the "great inventor" of glam, given earlier developments by artists like Marc Bolan and Joe Brieaz. "Joe Brieaz posiblemente no tenía ese gran talento que tenía David Bowie."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Tras los inicios del Glam. Jobriath

podcast.title: Tape Disposal
podcast.body: The speaker, after realizing the interview was unrecorded, pulled the cassette tape from his car's machine and threw it out onto the 401 highway, somewhere around Kipling and Keel. "I pulled it out of the cassette machine in my car and threw it on the 401s somewhere somewhere around Kipling, Keel."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: OGHONM 1000th Episode: The Q&A From the Live Recording

podcast.title: Terminal Illness Kept Secret
podcast.body: During the recording of Black Star, David Bowie was suffering from a terminal illness, a fact known only to his long-time producer and friend, Tony Visconti. The other musicians and collaborators involved in the project were not aware of his condition, which contributed to difficulties in the recording process. "Nadie durante la grabación era consciente del estado de enfermedad terminal que tenía David Bowie, el único que lo sabía era Donnie Visconti porque era un gran amigo personal de David Bowie pero el resto no lo sabía."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: The "Lost Decade" of the 90s
podcast.body: The 1990s were largely considered a "lost decade" for Bowie's career, as his attempts to recreate past success ("Black Tie White Noise") struggled with distribution and a changing music landscape. His most notable successes came from dabbling in techno and industrial music, like "Real Cool World" and "Outside." "In short, the 90s was something of a lost decade for Bowie."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: The "Real" Berlin Trilogy Theory
podcast.body: A theory suggests that the true "Berlin Trilogy" might not solely consist of Bowie's three albums, but rather David Bowie's *Low*, Iggy Pop's *The Idiot*, and Brian Eno's *Music For Airports*. This perspective accounts for the intense collaborative spirit and the fact that many of Bowie's recordings were not exclusively made in Berlin. "que posiblemente la gran trilogia de Berlin no eran los tres iscos de David Bowie sino que posiblemente la gran trilogia de Berlin fue el giro de David Bowie, fue ese de Hip-Hop y fue el mi-sik foro por Zebrai a Gennos, que posiblemente esos sí que fueron los tres grandes iscos que salieron de la trilogia de Berlin."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: David Bowie: La trilogía de Berlin 1

podcast.title: The 1980s: A Difficult Decade
podcast.body: The 1980s, beginning officially after *Lodger*, were not an easy or the best decade for David Bowie's career, despite producing major hits. He experienced creative and stylistic struggles and underwent aggressive changes in his image. "Los 80 la verdad es que no fueron una de cada fácil para David Bowie, nos dejó grandes éxitos, nos dejó grandes hits, pero no fue ni la mejor ni la más fácil que etapa de su carrera."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: David Bowie: La trilogía de Berlin 3

podcast.title: The Aladdin Sane Persona
podcast.body: This persona represented a twist on Bowie's alien image, leading to an even more iconic look, famously depicted on the 'Aladdin Sane' album cover. The cover featured a bear-chested, flame-haired Bowie with distinctive lightning bolt face makeup and a teardrop pooling in his collarbone. "If you know one Bowie album cover, it's probably this one. Bear Chested, Flame-haired David, with lightning bolt face makeup, a teardrop pooling in his collarbone."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: The Berlin Wall as a Metaphor
podcast.body: During the recording of *Heroes* at Hansa Studios, the omnipresent Berlin Wall served as a powerful visual metaphor that complemented the album's visual and emotional atmosphere. "David Bowie y Breyánino encontraron en el muro omnipresente durante toda la grabación, una meta fuera visual que complementaba la atmósfera visual y motiva del álbum."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: El proyecto que salvó a David Bowie. La trilogía de Berlín

podcast.title: The Greek Newspaper Ruse
podcast.body: Bowie reportedly employed a clever trick to avoid recognition when leaving his apartment: he would carry a Greek newspaper under his arm. If someone suspected his identity, seeing the foreign paper would often lead them to dismiss the idea, thinking he was "just some Greek man." "Bowie had this thing when he left the building. He'd have a Greek newspaper under his arm, and when someone might say, hey, isn't that David Bowie? Then they'd see the newspaper and say, oh, well, I guess it can't be. It's just some Greek man on his way for us who's lucky."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: The Thin White Duke Persona
podcast.body: During the *Station to Station* era, David Bowie embodied the character of the Thin White Duke, a persona so intertwined with his declining mental state that it was unclear where the character ended and his own madness began. This figure made controversial, "Nazi, racistas, totalitarios" comments, highlighting a man completely "out of control" who had "hit rock bottom." "Como él también se había creado ese nuevo personaje, el Granduke nos sabemos que parte era del personaje que se había inventado y que parte era su propia locura."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: The Thin White Duke Persona
podcast.body: Introduced in the lyrics of the title track from the 'Station to Station' album (1976), this character was associated with Bowie's especially gaunt appearance at the time. Bowie later claimed not to remember anything about the album's creation due to his raging addiction during this period. "This was the LP where he introduced the aforementioned Thin White Duke character in the lyrics of Station to Station's title track."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: The Thin White Duke Persona
podcast.body: David Bowie is known by the nickname "Thin White Duke," which is mentioned as a way to refer to him before a song about him is played. "let's just hear a little bit about the thin white duke."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: The Thin White Duke Persona
podcast.body: The "Station to Station" era was defined by Bowie's "Thin White Duke" persona, a character described as hollow, amoral, emotionless, and damaged, yet elegantly dressed in a white shirt and waistcoat. "Station to Station was the era of his thin white duke face."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: The Thin White Duke Persona - Thomas Jerome Newton Influence
podcast.body: This amoral, hollow, damaged, and emotionless character, with his signature white shirt and waistcoat, emerged from an autobiography Bowie began while filming "The Man Who Fell to Earth," in which he played the doomed space alien Thomas Jerome Newton. Bowie loved the character and asked to keep the costuming, directly influencing his look for the next couple of years. "This character came from a sort of autobiography Bowie had begun while filming the man who fell to Earth, the movie where he played a doomed space alien named Thomas Jerome Newton."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: The White Duke's Legacy
podcast.body: Bowie is visualized as "the White Duke," fading into the city he left behind, whistling melodies like a solitary hero who redefined his era's musical landscape, leaving an indelible mark. "Me encanta visualizar la figura del duque blanco, desbandeciéndose en la ciudad que dejó atrás, silbando alguna de esos melodías, como un héroes solitario que redifina el paisaje musical de su época."

srcs.source: Central Sonora

podcast.title: The Ziggy Stardust Persona
podcast.body: Four years after "Space Oddity," Bowie transformed himself into the orange-haired glam rock alien character, Ziggy Stardust, for the album 'The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust and The Spiders from Mars'. This alter ego became his image-making breakthrough, solidifying his quirky space cadet image. "Basically, four years after Space Audity Bowie had turned himself into the glam rock alien."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: The Ziggy Stardust Persona
podcast.body: Introduced in 1972, Ziggy Stardust became Bowie's most famous character, transforming the course of rock music. Ziggy was a doomed, drug-addled, glam spaceman, drawing inspiration from figures like Andy Warhol, Lou Reed, Bob Dylan, Frank Sinatra, and an obscure American singer named Vince Taylor. The character was described as part *Clockwork Orange* and part autobiography. Ziggy, performing with his band The Spiders From Mars, existed for only two years but became an enduring rock and roll icon, subject to books, PhD dissertations, and debates by scholars. Bowie's unique use of image and theater made Ziggy one of the most profound inventions in rock history, inspiring British kids bored with mainstream rock to create punk rock. "Bowie called his creation Ziggy Star Dust."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Theatrical Concert Tours
podcast.body: Bowie's concert tours were renowned for being among the most theatrical and ambitious ever to be taken on the road, showcasing his elaborate stage presentations. "His concert tours were among the most theatrical and ambitious things ever taken on the road."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Theatrical Retirement of Ziggy Stardust
podcast.body: Despite the overwhelming success of the Ziggy Stardust character, Bowie decided the persona had run its course and sought to retire it. He chose to do so in a highly theatrical manner, bowing out at the peak of his fame at a concert in one of London's most famous rock venues. "Bowie had decided that his Ziggy character had run its course and it was time to get out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Theatrical and Fashion Impact of Ziggy Stardust
podcast.body: Bowie's Ziggy Stardust character revolutionized rock music through its theatricality, distinctive clothes, makeup, and overall presentation, blending hard rock with vaudeville, disposable pop with serious theater, and fashion with technology. Its "sexy and very sexual" nature was groundbreaking for its time, making cross-dressing and male makeup fashionable in the 1970s and inspiring millions to copy his haircut. "Bowie's character changed so much in terms of rock music. The theater, the clothes, the makeup, the presentation."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 1

podcast.title: Tony Visconti's Production
podcast.body: Tony Visconti is known for being David Bowie's producer, among many other artists. "Tony Visconti is, you probably know, David Bowie's producer Mark Bowlin and a lot of other great people."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Toronto Concert After Death
podcast.body: After Bowie's death, a planned concert in Toronto with the surviving members of his Spiders from Mars band proceeded. The mood at this show was described as "stunned," with plenty of denial evident among fans as the truth of his passing began to sink in. "I was at that Tuesday show in Toronto, and the word to describe the mood was stunned."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Touring Companion (Late 1980s)
podcast.body: After the release of her debut album, Sinead O'Connor quickly found herself on tour with David Bowie, alongside INXS, with the rhythm section of The Smiths in her band. "She quickly found herself on tour with inexess and David Bowie with Andy Warken, Mike Joyce, the rhythm section of the Smiths in her band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Touring as Keyboard Player
podcast.body: Bowie toured with Iggy Pop not as a headlining act, but humbly as the keyboard player in Iggy's backup band, showcasing his dedication to fostering Iggy's career. "And Bowie even toured with Iggy, not as a headline act, but just as the keyboard player in his backup band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About Iggy Pop

podcast.title: Transition to "Blue-Eyed Plastic Soul"
podcast.body: During the "Diamond Dogs" tour, Bowie began transitioning from his "spaceman" image to a more elegant, sophisticated look with shorter hair and tailored suits. This paralleled a shift in his musical interests towards American soul and R&B, leading to the smoother, funkier sound of "Young Americans." This endorsement of black music encouraged many of his fans to explore those genres. "Bowie became less space man and more elegant, shorter hair, tailored suits, an air of sophistication."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Transition to "Elegant" Persona
podcast.body: During the "Diamond Dogs" tour, fans observed Bowie undergoing a transition, moving from his "spaceman" image to a more elegant aesthetic. This included shorter hair, tailored suits, and an overall air of sophistication, reflecting a shift in both his personal style and musical direction towards American soul and R&B. "Bowie became less space man and more elegant. Elder hair, tailored suits and this air of sophistication."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Transition to Aladdin Sane
podcast.body: Around 1974, Bowie moved from his Ziggy Stardust persona to the Aladdin Sane character, which largely followed a similar glam-oriented trajectory. "we dumped a Ziggy for his Aladdin Sane character which continued down or less the same path."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: David Bowie's song co-written with Queen, which was not sampled but rather recreated and interpolated by Vanilla Ice in "Ice Ice Baby." "Vanilla Ice did not sample the Queen, David Bowie song under pressure for Ice Ice Baby."

podcast.title: Unilateral Decisions and Returning Grandeur (Late 1970s)
podcast.body: During the recording of *Lodger*, David Bowie made certain unilateral decisions, reflecting a returning sense of grandeur and a desire to create a very complex and ambitious project. This contrasted with Brian Eno's typically humble and discreet approach. "ciertas decisiones un y laterales de David Bowie durante los procesos de grabación, también se hace referencia a ciertos aire, es ya un tanto de la grandeza que volvía a tener David Bowie y que quería hacer de lo que era un proyecto muy complejo y muy ambicioso."

podcast.title: Unofficial YouTube Availability of Peter and the Wolf
podcast.body: The *Peter and the Wolf* narration is not available on popular streaming services such as Spotify. However, a dedicated fan has reportedly ripped the album from vinyl, separated it into individual tracks, and uploaded it to YouTube, making this rare historical curiosity accessible to a wider audience. "evidentemente esto no está en el Spotify pero lo que sí he encontrado es un tío muy flipado que se ha cogido el mi pelo se lo ha grabado se lo ha pasado a pistas y lo ha subido a youtube."

podcast.title: Unwritten Autobiography
podcast.body: Bowie had promised to write his autobiography one day, but he sadly ran out of time before he could fulfill this promise. "One of the saddest things is that Bowie never got around to writing his autobiography."

podcast.title: Use of Accompanying Bands
podcast.body: Bowie is mentioned as an artist who had accompanying bands, implying a leader-focused structure rather than a purely solid, united band unit. This comparison is used to describe the current perception of the Arctic Monkeys' live performances. "Parecía más una banda de acompañamiento como las que tuvo David Bowie."

podcast.title: Visconti and Moss Inspiration for "Heroes"
podcast.body: Producer Tony Visconti provided a long-standing explanation for the lyrics of "Heroes," stating that David Bowie saw him embracing German singer Antonia Moss by the Berlin Wall. Visconti, from the West, and Moss, from the East, were depicted as hating the divided city but insisting on kissing by the wall as bullets flew from guard towers. Bowie later confirmed seeing the couple. "We've been told that one of the lovers is from the west, which is Visconti, and the other from the east, which is Moss."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Visionary Capabilities
podcast.body: David Bowie was a documented visionary, accurately predicting the rise of phenomena such as digital music, social media, and gender fluidity. This aspect of his career is used by some to support the more outlandish claim that he could also have predicted the rise of Kanye West. "Now, it is true that Bowie was a documented visionary when it came to predicting the rise of things like digital music and social media and gender fluidity."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Visit to Iggy Pop
podcast.body: Bowie was Iggy Pop's only visitor during his stay in a mental hospital, notably bringing him drugs. "By the way, his only visitor was David Bowie. He brought him drugs, but that's another story entirely."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Visited Iggy During Hospitalization
podcast.body: David Bowie was one of only two visitors Iggy Pop received during his weeks-long detoxification and psychiatric evaluation at the UCLA Neuropsychiatric Hospital in October 1974. "He had two visitors. One was David Bowie and the other was Bowie's costume designer, a woman named Ola Hudson."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

podcast.title: Vogue Magazine Inspiration for Ziggy's Hair
podcast.body: After deciding on a new look, David and Angie Bowie searched fashion magazines, eventually finding a version of the desired "new hair thing" in a Vogue advertisement, which served as the blueprint for Ziggy's iconic style. "It was then that neither Bowie or Angie, nobody remembers who, found a version of this new hair thing in an ad in Vogue magazine."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Widespread Musical Appeal
podcast.body: Bowie's music had such widespread appeal that it was played across diverse radio formats, including Top 40 stations and rock stations. It was considered "cool" in punk clubs, and his songs like "Fame" or "Young Americans" were often mixed in with dance music at disco venues, demonstrating his broad influence across genres. "And Bowie's cache had so much widespread appeal that his music was played on both top 40 stations and rock stations."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Wish to Compose Exit Music (For a Film)
podcast.body: David Bowie once confessed that *Exit Music (For a Film)* was the song he had always wished he could have composed himself. However, he also admitted that he felt he was not talented enough to have written such a piece. This remark stands as his most explicit acknowledgment of his admiration for Radiohead found in his interviews. "He referred to it on one occasion as the song he would have loved to have composed but wasn't good enough to have made."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Radiohead - Exit Music For a film tiene una historia un tanto curiosa

podcast.title: Ziggy Stardust - Breakthrough and Theatricality
podcast.body: The creation of Ziggy Stardust brought Bowie out of almost a decade of obscurity, elevating rock's theatricality to new levels. The character was presented as a "doomed spaceman with a Messiah concept," potentially involved in populating Earth with "Japanese style kabuki actors." Bowie used Ziggy to explore fashion, utilize his professional mime training from the 1960s, and experiment with art and sexuality. "this was the move that brought Bowie out of obscurity after almost a decade of dead ends."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

podcast.title: Ziggy Stardust - Theatrical Rock Star Persona
podcast.body: Bowie created Ziggy Stardust as a "doomed pansexual alien," using his acting and mime lessons to embody this character fully. This allowed him to sing, say, and do things he couldn't as "plain David Bowie." Ziggy's impact on rock in 1972 was immense, challenging the prevailing jeans and T-shirts aesthetic with makeup, costumes, and theatrical concerts featuring choreography, transforming rock into a full, immersive experience. "This idea of coming up with a pre-packaged synthetic ultra glamorous, ultra theatrical rock star."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ziggy Stardust Alter-Ego
podcast.body: Ziggy Stardust was one of David Bowie's first and most enduring alter-egos and stage characters, described as a "bisexual alien dressed up all in glitter." This persona was immensely popular in England in late 1972 and early 1973, with the whole country talking about him. "Ziggy Stardust, one of Bowie's first and most enduring of all his alter-egos and stage characters, had been the ticket."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ziggy Stardust Alter-Ego
podcast.body: Ziggy Stardust was one of Bowie's first and most enduring alter-egos and stage characters. Described as a "bisexual alien dressed up all in glitter," this persona was the primary driver of Bowie's immense popularity in England during late 1972 and 1973, with the entire country discussing him. "Ziggy Stardust, one of Bowie's first and most enduring of all his alter-egos and stage characters, had been the ticket."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ziggy Stardust Character's Impact
podcast.body: Bowie's Ziggy Stardust character offered significant hope to many, presenting himself as a weirdly androgynous, potentially bisexual figure who wore makeup and glitter and performed provocative acts on stage, such as simulating oral sex with his guitarist, Mick Ronson. Despite Bowie himself not being 100% gay, the character's persona profoundly impacted and inspired closeted people worldwide. "Ziggy was this weirdly androgynous, maybe bisexual creature who wore makeup and glitter and did all kinds of looed things on stage, like simulating oral sex in his guitarist, Mick Ronson."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Early Days of LGBTQ Rock

podcast.title: Ziggy Stardust Costume Inspiration
podcast.body: Ziggy Stardust's costumes drew inspiration from the main characters of Stanley Kubrick's controversial film *A Clockwork Orange*, which was banned in the UK for its depictions of violence and sex, as well as from Japanese designer Yasuko Hayashi. "Ziggy's clothes were inspired in equal parts by what we saw with the main characters in the film, a clockwork orange... And a Japanese designer named Yasuko Hayashi."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

podcast.title: Ziggy Stardust Hairdo Creation
podcast.body: Bowie's iconic "Ziggy Stardust puff ball" hairstyle, a striking mullet, was conceived from photos in a fashion magazine called Honey (for the front) and French Vogue (for the back and sides). His mother's stylist, Susie Fussy, from Evelyn Page salon, helped create it, dyeing it "Schwartzkoft red" and stiffening it with an anti-dandruff treatment called Guard. This unisex haircut became a defining style of the era. "They created the famous Ziggy Stardust puff ball."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ziggy Stardust Inspiration
podcast.body: David Bowie's iconic Ziggy Stardust character was partly inspired by the American singer Vince Taylor, known for his 1959 song "Brand New Cadillac." "The original was by Vince Taylor, an American singer who provided part of the inspiration for David Bowie's Ziggy Stardust character."

podcast.title: Ziggy Stardust Persona
podcast.body: Bowie immersed himself fully into the persona of Ziggy Stardust, a "doomed pansexual alien." This character was a "pre-packaged synthetic ultra glamorous, ultra theatrical, fantastical rock star" that fundamentally changed the presentation of rock music. srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ziggy Stardust Tour Theatricality
podcast.body: The tour supporting "The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust and The Spiders from Mars" (January 29, 1972 - July 3, 1973) set a new standard for theatricality in rock, incorporating "big end themic songs, costume changes, choreography, makeup, tall boots, and ridiculously high platform shoes" along with "daring sexual ambiguity." "the tour, which ran from January 29th, 1972 to July 3rd, 1973, was the most theatrical thing that rock had ever seen to that point."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

podcast.title: Ziggy Stardust and Mullet Popularization
podcast.body: David Bowie's debut of the Ziggy Stardust character gave a jump start to the mullet hairstyle in the late 1960s. The mullet, having been largely invisible, was then seen as a radical, scary, and shocking look, contributing to its spread across society. "When David Bowie's debut of the Ziggy Stardust character gave it a jump start, the mullet was seen as radical and scary and shocking."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ziggy Stardust's Cultural Impact
podcast.body: Through his "weirdly androgynous Ziggy Stardust character," David Bowie became one of the most influential alternative artists of all time. Ziggy Stardust shattered the myth of the "hetero-metro rock star with the guitar," proving that a performer could be sexually ambiguous and still achieve significant commercial success.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ziggy Stardust's Orange Puffball Haircut
podcast.body: Around eight years after his early advocacy, Bowie, heavily influenced by his wife Angie, debuted the iconic orange puffball with a tail haircut, which became central to his Ziggy Stardust persona and is regarded as one of rock's most influential hairstyles. "The orange puffball with a tail, sported by Bowie and his Ziggy Stardust face."

Ziggy Stardust Debut (July 8, 1972)
concerts.body: David Bowie debuted his Ziggy Stardust persona on stage at the Royal Festival Hall in London on July 8, 1972, introducing himself by saying, "Hi, I'm Ziggy." This marked the beginning of Ziggy Stardust's 360-day public lifespan. "That night, David Bowie stepped on stage at the Royal Festival Hall in London and introduced himself by saying, hi, I'm Ziggy."

concerts.title: Hammersmith Odeon (July 3rd, 1973) – Ziggy Stardust Retirement
concerts.body: This infamous London concert, captured by documentary filmmaker DA Pennebaker, was David Bowie's "quits show." It marked the last show of the tour and the final performance of the Ziggy Stardust persona, concluding an extraordinary period in British rock. "The infamous Bowie quits show at the Hammersmith Odeon in London July 3rd 1973."

concerts.title: Station to Station Tour (1976)
concerts.body: During this tour, David Bowie displayed his deep admiration for the German electronic band Kraftwerk by playing recordings and video projections of their album *Radio-Activity*. This demonstrated his interest in the Kraurock sound that would later influence his "Berlin Trilogy." "durante los conciertos del station to station. David Bowie ponía grabaciones y video proyecciones del radioactividad de Crabbro porque tenía una gran sesión con Crabbro."

xref.title: Glam Rock Catalyst (1971)
xref.body: In March 1971, T-Rex appeared on the hugely important British TV show "Top of the Pops." During this performance, Marc Bolan, the band's frontman, wore satin clothes and was covered with glitter dust, an event that David Bowie watched at home and found "brilliant," marking it as "the beginning of glam rock" and inspiring Bowie to pursue a similar direction. "In March 1971, T-Rex appeared on top of the pops, the hugely important British TV show."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Glam Rock Pioneer (1971)
xref.body: Marc Bolan, a former rival who became friends with David Bowie, was a key figure in the emergence of glam rock. In March 1971, he appeared on "Top of the Pops" wearing satin clothes and covered with glitter dust, an appearance that profoundly inspired David Bowie. "Bowie had become friends with Mark Bowlin, a former foe he would take an up electric guitars and formed a psych band called T-Rex."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Meeting David Bowie (September 7, 1971)
xref.body: While in New York "sponging off a friend," Iggy Pop met David Bowie on September 7, 1971. Bowie, who was on the verge of launching his Ziggy Stardust phase, was influenced by Iggy, choosing the name Ziggy partly due to Iggy's persona. "The date was September 7th of 1971. Bowie was about to launch into his Ziggy stardust phase. That character was to be in part inspired by Iggy."

xref.title: Peele Session with David Bowie (May 23rd, 1972)
xref.body: The Spiders from Mars, as David Bowie's band, participated in a "Peele Session" on May 23rd, 1972. These sessions, overseen by DJ John Peel at the BBC, were a significant platform for artists to perform and record live, especially during periods of "Needle Time" restrictions. "Here's something from May 23rd, 1972, when an artist on the asset named David Bowie dropped in for a session with his band, The Spiders from Mars."

xref.title: Elton John Gorilla Suit Incident – Richards, Atlanta, October 1973
xref.body: In October 1973, Iggy Pop and the Stooges were playing at Richards in Atlanta at the same time Elton John was touring America. Elton — engaged in a semi-friendly rivalry with David Bowie, who was a known Stooges supporter — decided to crash the show dressed in a full gorilla suit to surprise Iggy on stage. A photographer from Detroit music magazine *Creem* was tipped off. No one warned Iggy that this was planned, and no one warned Elton that Iggy was heavily intoxicated on speed that night. When Elton bounded onto the stage in the gorilla suit, Iggy genuinely believed it was a real gorilla, was terrified, and fled the stage. The incident was captured on film. After Elton removed the gorilla head and multiple people calmed Iggy down, the show resumed and the two performed several songs together — Iggy bare-chested, Elton still in the suit. "Iggy thought it was an actual gorilla. And this freak out is captured on film."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Elton John's Attempted Signing and Gorilla Prank (1973)
xref.body: Elton John, in a competitive rivalry with David Bowie, attempted to show support for and potentially sign The Stooges to his new record label. This led to a surprise visit where Elton, in a gorilla suit, crashed their stage in October 1973, startling Iggy Pop who was heavily under the influence of Quaaludes. "Elton thought he'd have a little fun with Bowie and his relationship with the Stooges, and in the process, maybe he could sign them to his new record label."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Gorilla Suit Stage Crash (1973)
xref.body: In October 1973, Elton John, intending to prank David Bowie and potentially sign The Stooges, donned a rented gorilla suit and bounded onto the stage during a Stooges performance at Richard's Club in Atlanta. He surprised an already drug-addled Iggy Pop, who mistook him for a real gorilla, and nearly got into a fight with James Williamson before revealing his identity. "Elton John dressed in a gorilla suit, bounds on stage."

xref.title: Theft of Bowie's Gear (1973)
xref.body: On July 2nd, 1973, after David Bowie's final Ziggy Stardust tour show at the Hammersmith Odeon Theatre in London, a young Steve Jones managed to get inside the building and steal microphones and amps. These stolen items would later be used by Jones to start his new band, the Sex Pistols, a couple of years later. "A young thief named Steve Jones somehow got inside and helped himself to whatever he could carry out, mostly some microphones and some amps."

xref.title: Theft of Bowie's Gear (July 1973)
xref.body: As a young thief in July 1973, Steve Jones broke into the Hammersmith Odeon during a David Bowie and The Spiders from Mars' engagement and stole microphones and amplifiers. xref.title: Move to West Berlin with David Bowie (Post-1976)
xref.body: Iggy Pop, seeking sobriety, moved to West Berlin with David Bowie after Bowie's period of intense drug addiction and paranoia. They both aimed to clean up and dry out in the city. xref.title: Regeneration in West Berlin (May 1976)
xref.body: In late May 1976, Iggy Pop moved to West Berlin with David Bowie to escape their destructive lifestyles in Los Angeles and to regenerate among the city's diverse community of bohemians, weirdos, drug addicts, prostitutes, and transsexuals. This move, prompted by Bowie's heart attack scare in the fall of 1976, led both artists to seriously clean up their acts and embark on an incredibly creative period. "So in late May 1976, Bowie and Iggy moved to West Berlin to regenerate in the company of the Bohemians and weirdos and drug addicts and prostitutes and transsexuals who lived there."

xref.title: Death in Car Accident (1977)
xref.body: Mark Bolan, a famous British glam musician and friend of David Bowie, was killed instantly on September 16, 1977, when the Mini he owned, driven by his girlfriend Gloria Jones, crashed. Bolan never learned to drive because he feared dying in a car accident. He had other, larger cars available, including a Rolls-Royce he had lent out to another band that night. xref.title: Feedback Loops for David Bowie (1977)
xref.body: In 1977, Robert Fripp was brought in to collaborate with David Bowie for his "Heroes" album in Berlin, with the sole instruction to "do something weird" for the title track. Fripp created three distinct feedback loops: an A note fed back four feet from the amplifier, a G note fed back three feet from the amp, and a similar third take. All these guitar feedback tracks were then processed through an EMS synthesizer, a keyboard-less synth about the size of a briefcase, contributing a unique distorted and feedback-laden texture to Bowie's song. "Three takes, all based on feedback loops."

xref.title: Rumored Affair with David Bowie (1990)

xref.title: Tom Verlaine Death (January 28, 2023) – Prostate Cancer, Age 73; Helped CBGB Become Ground Zero for Punk
xref.body: Tom Verlaine co-founded Television and in 1973 helped Hilly Kristal — owner of a scuzzy bar on Bleecker Street in a then-terrible part of New York — to let Television play a Sunday night residency. This decision catalyzed CBGB into becoming ground zero for New York punk and, by chain reaction, the entire international punk movement. Television produced two critically acclaimed albums before breaking up in 1978. Verlaine subsequently collaborated with Patti Smith, worked with James Iha of the Smashing Pumpkins, had a song covered by David Bowie, and was involved in a 1992 Television reunion album. He was scheduled to produce Jeff Buckley's second album — a project ended when Buckley drowned in the Mississippi River in 1997. Verlaine was diagnosed with prostate cancer at some point in the 2000s; it metastasized. He died January 28, 2023, age 73. "That was the catalyst for making CBGB ground zero for the world of New York punk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

He also shaped the distinctive sound of The Cars and worked with artists ranging from David Bowie to Metallica and Guns N' Roses. xref.title: Bowie's Admiration and Support
xref.body: David Bowie considered Iggy Pop one of his musical heroes, captivated by Iggy's craziness, mental instability, and intelligence that Bowie saw beyond the drug use and wild stage persona. Bowie became Iggy's patron, securing funding for The Stooges' *Raw Power* album. When Iggy eventually ended up in a mental hospital after the band's collapse, Bowie was his only visitor. "Bowie saw that Iggy was actually very, very intelligent."

xref.title: Bowie's Fascination
xref.body: David Bowie remained fascinated with "The Legendary Stardust Cowboy" and his music until Bowie's own death, despite not meeting Norm O'Dam until 1998. This enduring fascination underscores the profound impact Norm's outsider art had on a major mainstream icon. "By the way, David Bowie never met the man until 1998, and he remained fascinated with him until his death."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Bowie's Influence on Depeche Mode
xref.body: Depeche Mode showed clear influences of David Bowie's work, particularly in the realm of goth music and electronic sounds. Bowie's legacy as a pioneer in electronic and genre-bending music resonated with bands like Depeche Mode. "You could see lots of Bowie influence in Depeche Mode and the cure and new order."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Bowie's Influence on New Order
xref.body: New Order showcased considerable influence from David Bowie, particularly in their electronic and New Wave soundscapes. Bowie's pioneering use of electronics in the 1970s and his consistent push for rock to progress left a clear mark on bands like New Order. "You could see lots of Bowie influence in Depeche Mode and the cure and new order."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Bowie's Influence on The Cure
xref.body: The Cure exhibited significant influence from David Bowie, particularly evident in their goth and post-punk aesthetics. Bowie's exploration of dark themes, theatricality, and genre fluidity provided inspiration for bands like The Cure. "You could see lots of Bowie influence in Depeche Mode and the cure and new order."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Bowie's Intervention and *Raw Power* Production
xref.body: David Bowie, then on a hot streak with significant industry power, bonded with Iggy Pop. He convinced Iggy, Ron and Scott Ashton, and James Williamson to move to England to record *Raw Power* for Columbia Records, effectively resurrecting the band. "Bowie was on a hot streak and thus he had power. And after bonding with Iggy, he convinced him, the Ashton brothers in James Williamson, to come to England where they'd all make a record for Columbia Records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

xref.title: Bowie's Role in Career Rebirth
xref.body: David Bowie not only got Iggy Pop a new management deal and a record contract but also actively collaborated on his first two solo albums, The Idiot and Lust for Life, and even toured as his backup keyboard player. This intervention was pivotal in Iggy's career comeback. "Thanks to Bowie Iggy's career was reborn."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About Iggy Pop

xref.title: Bowie's Support During Hospitalization
xref.body: During Iggy Pop's hospitalization in 1974, he had only two visitors: David Bowie and Bowie's costume designer, Ola Hudson (mother of Saul Hudson, later known as Slash). Bowie, despite his own struggles with drugs, played a crucial role as Iggy's and ultimately The Stooges' savior. "He had two visitors. One was David Bowie and the other was Bowie's costume designer, a woman named Ola Hudson."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Catalog Sale to Harbor View Equity Partners
xref.body: Deryck Whibley sold his song catalog, specifically the songs he wrote for Sum 41, to Harbor View Equity Partners. The exact amount was not disclosed, but he "smiled very, very, very widely" when asked, suggesting a significant payout. "Derek Wibley's song is written for some 41. Another important development of the field of putting song catalogs to work came in 1997, when David Bowie and an investment banker named David Pullman created a financial instrument called Bowie Bonds. To use Wall Street speak, 287 songs from 25 albums recorded before 1990 became asset-backed securities. In exchange for forfeiting royalty income for a period of 10 years, Bowie received an immediate payment of $55 million. He used that money to buy out the rights to songs he lost to his former manager, Tony DeFrees."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Championed by David Bowie
xref.body: David Bowie acted as an educator for Lou Reed, helping to spread awareness and appreciation for his work. Through his advocacy and collaborations, Bowie brought attention to otherwise obscure performers like Reed, contributing to their wider recognition. "And through his work with Iggy Pop and Lou Reed, and through his early championing of the Velvet Underground, Bowie acted as an educator, a person who helped spread the word on these otherwise obscure performers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Championed by David Bowie
xref.body: David Bowie was an early champion of The Velvet Underground, playing a significant role as an "educator" who helped spread the word about this otherwise obscure performer and band. His advocacy contributed to their eventual recognition and influence within music. "And through his work with Iggy Pop and Lou Reed, and through his early championing of the Velvet Underground, Bowie acted as an educator, a person who helped spread the word on these otherwise obscure performers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Collaboration with Bowie on "Young Americans"
xref.body: John Lennon collaborated with David Bowie during his "last week in the Strangement" from Yoko Ono, co-writing the lyrics for the song "Fame" in about 20 minutes. He also provided background vocals, notably echoing the word "fame" in the verses of the recording for Bowie's "Young Americans" album. Lennon and Bowie got along famously, and Lennon's assistant, May Pang, later married Bowie's producer, Tony Visconti. "Not only did he and Bowie get along famously but so did Lennon's assistant May Pang and Bowie producer Tony Viscante and they actually ended up getting married."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Collaboration with David Bowie
xref.body: As David Bowie's Spiders From Mars guitarist, Mick Ronson collaborated with Bowie to produce Lou Reed's 1972 album, *Transformer*. Their work helped Reed find a new sound, demonstrating Ronson's influence beyond his guitar playing. "Bowie and his spiders from Mars guitarist, Mick Ronson, helped Lou find a new sound."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Collaboration with David Bowie
xref.body: David Bowie, after seeing Klaus Nomi perform live, was so impressed that he invited Nomi to collaborate. This led to Nomi's appearance with Bowie on Saturday Night Live on December 15, 1979, where he provided backup vocals on three songs. "And that led to Nomi's appearance with Bowie on Saturday Night Live. The date was December 15, 1979. He sang back up on three songs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Collaboration with David Bowie
xref.body: Reznor's admiration for Bowie led to collaborations, including touring together and Reznor's appearance in the "creepy stalker" music video for Bowie's 1997 song "I'm Afraid of Americans." Nine Inch Nails also contributed a remix of the song. "So much so that not only did they tour together, but Bowie also got trend to appear in the creepy stalker video for this song from 1997."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Collaboration with David Bowie in Berlin
xref.body: In 1977, Iggy Pop was in Berlin with David Bowie, cleaning up and detoxing, during which time the song "Lust for Life" was created. "The track dates back to 1977 when Iggy was cleaning up and drying out and detoxing in Berlin with his buddy David Bowie."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Collaborations and Film Role (Late 1980s)
xref.body: Between the ages of 16 and 20, Sinead's career accelerated rapidly. She co-wrote and recorded with The Edge, toured with INXS and David Bowie (with Andy Rourke and Mike Joyce of The Smiths in her band), had songs placed in movies, and starred in a Northern Irish film called *Hasha-Veibaby*. "She performed on David Letterman, participated in more collaborations with other artists, had her songs placed in movies. And she starred in a movie from Northern Ireland called Hasha-Veibaby."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Collaborations and Influence
xref.body: Arcade Fire recorded and toured with legendary artist David Bowie, and their music was used by U2 as entrance music for a tour, indicating their high regard among influential musicians. "They recorded in tour with David Bowie. You too use one of their songs as entrance music for a tour."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Collapse and Iggy's Hospitalization
xref.body: Following their struggles, The Stooges couldn't maintain cohesion, leading to their eventual collapse. This period saw Iggy Pop's personal struggles escalate, resulting in him ending up in a mental hospital. David Bowie, a devoted admirer and patron, was Iggy's sole visitor during this time. "Of course, the Stooges couldn't hold it together and everything collapsed. Iggy eventually ended up at a mental hospital, where his only visitor was, you guessed it, David Bowie."

xref.title: David Bowie Prediction Theory
xref.body: A conspiracy theory suggests that David Bowie predicted Kanye West's rise to stardom in 1972, five years before his birth. Evidence cited includes the "K. West" sign on Bowie's *Ziggy Stardust* album cover, the song "Five Years" from that album, and the title of Bowie's final album, *Black Star*, which is interpreted as an "anointment" of Kanye as a "Black Star." Kanye West was also among the first to pay tribute to Bowie on Twitter after his death, and stories circulated about Kanye planning a Bowie tribute album. "David Bowie allegedly predicting the birth of Kanye West back in 1972, five years before it actually happened."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: David Bowie's Advocacy
xref.body: David Bowie became a significant fan of Bauhaus and actively lobbied for the band to be cast in his vampire movie, "The Hunger." Their performance of "Bela Lugosi's Dead" was featured in a scene filmed at the London club Heaven. "David Bowie had become a big fan and he lobbied for the band to be cast in a vampire movie he was doing called The Hunger."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.body: Despite their struggle for commercial success across four albums before disbanding in 1975, Fanny garnered high praise from David Bowie, who considered them "brilliant." "Like I said, Bowie thought they were brilliant."
