xref.title: David Bowie's Intervention
xref.body: David Bowie, who had admired Iggy Pop's energy for years and even wrote a song about him in 1972, was the only person who cared enough to visit Iggy during his psychiatric confinement. Bowie "finally convinced Iggy that he didn't need to kill himself," thereby playing a crucial role in his career's rebirth. "Bowie was the only person in the world who cared about what happened to Iggy Pop and it was him who finally convinced Iggy that he didn't need to kill himself."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About Iggy Pop

xref.title: David Bowie's Praise
xref.body: David Bowie openly stated that the Langley kids' version of "Space Oddity" was one of the best interpretations of his songs he had ever heard. This endorsement highlighted the unique charm and sincerity with which the choir performed, despite any technical shortcomings. "And David Bowie went on record as saying that this is one of the best interpretations that he has ever heard of one of his songs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Detox and Berlin Relocation
xref.body: Following his arrest and hospitalization in October 1974, Iggy Pop, with support from David Bowie, moved to Berlin. There, they both cleaned up their drug habits and restarted their careers, with Iggy launching his solo career in 1977. "Iggy and Bowie moved to Berlin, cleaned up and restarted their careers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

xref.title: Detrimental Managerial Contract with David Bowie
xref.body: From the early 1970s, Tony DeFrees had a "terrible arrangement" as David Bowie's manager, which left Bowie financially "skint" despite his numerous platinum albums and chart-topping singles. Although Bowie left DeFrees in 1975, the contract allowed DeFrees to continue collecting royalties on Bowie's records until 1996. "Seeing the early 70s, he entered a terrible arrangement with manager Tony DeFrees, and even with all the platinum albums and chart-topping singles, he was close to Skint, he had nothing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Diehard David Bowie Fan
xref.body: Trent Reznor is described as a "diehard Bowie fan" who greatly admires David Bowie's work and influence, especially in industrial music. "Trent and Rizner was and always will be a diehard Bowie fan."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Drug Abuse and Psychiatric Care (Pre-Berlin)
xref.body: Prior to his move to West Berlin, Iggy Pop was deeply entrenched in heroin and LSD abuse, leading him to spend a considerable amount of time in a psychiatric hospital. His only visitor during this challenging period was his friend, David Bowie, highlighting the severity of his condition and Bowie's supportive role. "Meanwhile, Iggy was so deep into heroin and LSD that he had spent a considerable amount of time in a psychiatric hospital where his only visitor was his friend, David Bowie."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 8

xref.title: Drug Session Hallucination
xref.body: During a drug session with David Bowie, Iggy Pop experienced a hallucination where he believed Bowie's TV was eating his girlfriend, inspiring Bowie to write the song "TVC-15." "Iggy thought that Bowie's TV was eating his girlfriend."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early 1970s Psychotic Break – Voluntary Psychiatric Commitment
xref.body: In the early 1970s, Iggy Pop spent a large record-label advance on drugs and suffered a psychotic episode. Given the choice between jail and a Los Angeles psychiatric institute, he voluntarily chose hospitalization. His only visitor during his stay was David Bowie, who was himself deeply immersed in his own drug haze at the time. "His only visitor was David Bowie, also immersed in his own drug fog."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early 1990s Glam Revival
xref.body: Suede, emerging in the early 1990s, immediately displayed clear influences from David Bowie, Roxy Music, and the broader glam rock movement, showing glam's continued presence. "When they showed up in the early 1990s, it took all of two seconds to understand that they were equal parts Bowie, Roxy, and Glam."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

xref.title: Early 80s Androgynous Makeup
xref.body: In the early 1980s, Depeche Mode was influential in popularizing androgynous makeup styles among male musicians. This aesthetic contributed to the diverse visual landscape of the new wave era. "Styles run from the over-the-top glam of David Bowie and the New York Dolls in the early 1970s to the androgynous styles of Depeche mode in the early 80s..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Directorial Work with Bowie
xref.body: Before achieving widespread fame, Ridley Scott directed an ice cream commercial in which David Bowie was cast, during a period when both individuals were trying to find their professional paths. "That commercial was directed by another guy trying to find his way. His name was Ridley Scott."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Gear from Bowie Theft
xref.body: When the Sex Pistols began rehearsing and performing gigs in 1975, it is presumed that some of their initial equipment, including microphones and amplifiers, was stolen from David Bowie at the Hammersmith Odeon in July 1973 by their guitarist, Steve Jones. This gear would have been part of their early contributions to the punk rock era. "And when the pistols started rehearsing and playing gigs in 1975, it is very reasonable to assume that some of the gear that they were using to kick off their contributions to the punk rock era was all stolen from Bowie in 1972."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

xref.title: Early Goth Scene Inspiration
xref.body: The first version of Ultravox was recognized as one of the artists whose dark music helped attract punk refugees who were looking for a gloomier sound, contributing to the formation of the Goth scene. "That would include David Bowie and joint-evision, the first version of Ultravox, and an Irish performance art group called The Virgin Proons."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Goth Scene Inspiration
xref.body: The Virgin Prunes, an Irish performance art group, was mentioned as contributing dark music that attracted punk refugees and helped coalesce the early Goth scene. "That would include David Bowie and joint-evision, the first version of Ultravox, and an Irish performance art group called The Virgin Proons."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Influences
xref.body: Pat Smear's early listening habits, before punk rock, included progressive and mainstream rock artists like Yes, Queen, Alice Cooper, and David Bowie, alongside The Runaways. He later embraced punk rock when the scene became open to bands like The Germs who "didn't know how to play." "I was listening to yes. I was listening to Queen and a Alaskupper and David Bowie."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Influences & Recognition
xref.body: The Stooges are frequently cited as a major influence by contemporary bands like The White Stripes and The Hives, and by 90s bands such as Jane's Addiction and Nirvana. They also shaped the sound of 80s bands like Sonic Youth and inspired 70s artists like the Sex Pistols, Ramones, and David Bowie to make music. "So the stooges seem to be on everybody's list even though they hardly sold any records in their day and were so messed up that their singer ended up in an asylum."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

xref.title: Early Musical Influences
xref.body: Adam Slack's musical upbringing included The Rolling Stones (especially Keith Richards), 1970s Glam Rock artists like David Bowie and T. Rex, and the band Queen. "He grew up listening to the Rolling Stones, he loves Keith Richards, 70s Glam Rock from Bowie and T. Rex, and Queen."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Emerging as Producer
xref.body: After leaving Roxy Music, Brian Eno began to come into his own as a producer, contributing substantially to experimental projects like David Bowie's "Low." "Brian Eno, who had left rock-sea music and was really starting to come into his own as a producer."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Esteemed Fans and Original Songwriting
xref.body: Before their breakup in 1975, Fanny garnered a significant following that included David Bowie, John Lennon, George Harrison, and Sly Stone. They released five major label albums and notably wrote all their own songs, a rare feat for female artists at the time. "David Bowie, John and George from The Beatles, Slice Stone, and a ton of other big names became huge fans. They released five major label albums and they wrote all their own songs, which is something almost no female artists did back in those days."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Evolving Image
xref.body: Initially a tomboy, PJ Harvey adopted an approach similar to David Bowie in constantly transforming her image for almost every album project. This involved experimenting with both her clothing and physical appearance, often collaborating with her photographer friend, Maria Monachic. "PJ was originally very much a tomboy, but once she got started in the music business, she became almost bowie-esque with the way she changes her image for almost every album project."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Exile and Return to Music
xref.body: After leaving The Velvet Underground, Lou Reed spent over two years in exile at his parents' house on Long Island, where he quietly focused on writing poetry. In 1972, he ended this period and released a solo album that confused his record company, but David Bowie recognized his potential. "In 1972, Lou ended his exile at his parents' house on Long Island, where he had been quietly running poetry for more than two years after stomping out on the velvet."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Extensive Work as Designer
xref.body: Over the years, Willie Williams has worked with numerous famous artists, including R.E.M., David Bowie, The Rolling Stones, George Michael, and notably, U2, designing their tours. "And over the years, he's worked with R.E.M. David Bowie, the Rolling Stones, George Michael, and of course you two."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: We Are The Road Crew - A History of Roadies

xref.title: Extreme Performances
xref.body: The Stooges, featuring Iggy Pop, were known for their "extreme things" performed in America, contributing to the outrageous aesthetic that inspired David Bowie's Ziggy Stardust persona. "who was doing all kinds of extreme things in America with his band, The Stooges."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

xref.title: Fashion Victimness – David Bowie and Roxy Music Influence
xref.body: Sid was initially very focused on fashion, particularly styles inspired by David Bowie's Ziggy Stardust and Aladdin Sane periods. He was also a huge fan of Roxy Music and would steal Vogue magazines, often getting fashion details wrong. "He was really into clothes, especially the styles inspired by David Bowie through his Ziggy Stardust in the Latin St period."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Financial Windfall from China Girl
xref.body: Iggy Pop earned a significant amount of money, estimated close to a million dollars, from David Bowie's commercially successful cover version of "China Girl." Iggy had co-written the song, originally appearing on his 1977 album The Idiot. "In fact, a good guess would be somewhere close to a million dollars."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About Iggy Pop

xref.title: Flamboyance and Influence
xref.body: Despite performing as a Black and gay artist in the US South in the 1950s, Little Richard's flamboyance, energy, and music had a massive effect across rock and roll. His influence extended to artists like The Beatles, James Brown, David Bowie, and even Lemmy of Motorhead, reverberating through the entire genre. "His flamboyance, his energy, and his music reverberated through all of rock and roll."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Followed Bowie Bonds Model
xref.body: The Motown songwriting team of Holland-Dozier-Holland followed David Bowie's innovative financial model, utilizing intellectual property to secure financial instruments after the success of the Bowie Bonds. This demonstrated the broader impact of Bowie's pioneering business acumen in the music industry. "And once the Bowie bonds sold, others followed, including the Motown songwriting team of Holland-Doseyour Holland, as well as a number of other professional songwriters."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Foppish Fashion and Glam Rock Influence
xref.body: Unlike grunge bands, Suede embraced a foppish fashion sense. Singer Brett Anderson was a fan of David Bowie's glam rock period from the early 1970s, which by 1992, sounded fresh again. "Swade came with a sense of foppish fashion. Singer Brett Anderson was a fan of David Bowie's glam rock period of the early 1970s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

xref.title: Formation and Early Recognition
xref.body: A group of "precocious university students," influenced by artists like David Bowie, Roxy Music, and The Smiths, formed a band that would eventually be known as Suede (referred to in the transcript as "Swade"). After only a couple of gigs, they quickly achieved "next big thing status." "A bunch of precocious university students stopped listening to their Bowie, Roxy Music and Smith's records long enough to form a group called Swade. A couple of gigs brought them next big thing status."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Formation and Influence – Post-Drumming for Iggy Pop
xref.body: After his initial drumming experiences, Iggy Pop moved on from behind the drum kit to start writing songs and formed The Stooges. This band, along with Iggy's subsequent involvement with David Bowie and other experiences, contributed significantly to laying the foundations for modern punk rock. "He started writing songs moved on to the stooges got involved with David Bowie took a lot of LSD and pretty much laid the foundations for modern punk rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Formation as a Four-Piece Rock Band
xref.body: David Bowie formed Tin Machine with the explicit idea of creating a four-piece rock band where he would serve solely as the lead singer. This project was a conscious effort to flush away the baggage of his past hits and artistic personas, drawing inspiration from the raw aesthetics of bands like Jimi Hendrix, Cream, and the Pixies. "His idea was to form a four piece rock band with him just as the lead singer."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Fringe Status and Bowie's Admiration
xref.body: The Velvet Underground, featuring Lou Reed, occupied a position on the extreme fringes of the music scene, with little recognition outside of "Uber hipsters." Despite their obscurity, David Bowie was a great admirer of the band, particularly Lou Reed, recognizing their unique significance. "No one except the Uber hipsters gave a damn or even knew about Lou Reed in the velvet underground."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Glam Influence in New Wave
xref.body: The B-52s are cited as a new wave band whose music was influenced by glam rock, demonstrating North America's exposure to glam primarily through David Bowie. "It was enough to influence a plethora of new wave bands, I'm looking at you B-52s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

xref.title: Harsh Critical Reception
xref.body: The two albums released by Tin Machine between 1989 and 1991 received very harsh reviews. Critics often judged the band not only against David Bowie's celebrated past works but also against the rising tide of alternative music at the time, perceiving Bowie as an "old man trying to be hip again" with his rock band. "There would be two Tin Machine albums before the project was retired and during this time which would be between 1989 and 1991, they received some pretty harsh reviews."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: High-Profile Fans
xref.body: Arcade Fire counts prominent musicians like Bono, Peter Gabriel, and David Bowie among their admirers, highlighting their respected standing within the music community and influence among peers. "Fans include Bono and Peter Gabriel and David Bowie."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Who the Hell is Arcade Fire? Part 1

xref.title: Highly Respected by Famous Musicians
xref.body: Fanny garnered a significant following among prominent musicians, with huge fans including David Bowie, John Lennon and George Harrison from The Beatles, and Sly Stone, among many other big names in the industry. David Bowie even sent them a fan letter and spoke highly of them in interviews. "Before they broke up in 1975, David Bowie, John and George from the Beatles, Slice Stone, and a ton of other big names became huge fans."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Ian Curtis's Musical Preference
xref.body: Ian Curtis was a fan of The Doors, often preferring to stay home and listen to their records rather than attend school. "Ian would rather stay home with his books and Iggy Pop and Doors and David Bowie and Lou Reed records than go to class."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Iconic Band Leader
xref.body: Brian Ferry was the legendary leader of Roxy Music, recognized as one of the most stylish British bands of the mid to late 1970s. Roxy Music sold numerous records and provided inspiration to millions, often appealing to fans of David Bowie. "Brian Ferry was the legendary leader of Roxy Music, one of the most stylish of all the British bands of the middle and late 70s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock Star Kids ｜ From the Archives

xref.title: Impact of Bowie's "Coming Out"
xref.body: Boy George of Culture Club openly stated that his life was profoundly changed by David Bowie's public comments in January 1972 about being gay. Bowie's statement gave him the courage to embrace and be true to his own identity. "Boy George of Culture Club and Holly Johnson of Frankie Ghost of Hollywood say that their lives were changed by Bowie's comments."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Impact of Bowie's "Coming Out"
xref.body: Holly Johnson of Frankie Goes to Hollywood credited David Bowie's "coming out" statement in January 1972 as having changed his life. Bowie's public bravery gave Johnson the courage to be who he was. "Boy George of Culture Club and Holly Johnson of Frankie Ghost of Hollywood say that their lives were changed by Bowie's comments."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence from David Bowie
xref.body: The Smiths, particularly a young Morrissey and Johnny Marr from Manchester, were profoundly influenced by David Bowie, especially his album "Scary Monsters and Super Creeps." Bowie's impact on their formation and sound was so significant that it is suggested modern music, as it is known today, might not exist without his influence on them. "Again, a hugely influential album, especially on a young kid from Manchester named Morrissey and is soon to be mate Johnny Mar. Again, no Bowie, no Smiths."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence from David Bowie's Scary Monsters
xref.body: Both Stephen Patrick Morrissey and Johnny Marr were profoundly influenced by David Bowie's album "Scary Monsters and Super Creeps," to the extent that it's suggested The Smiths would not have existed without Bowie's influence. "No Bowie? No Smiths."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence of David Bowie
xref.body: The Foo Fighters' sound and vision contain "bits of Bowie DNA," indicating a clear influence from David Bowie's work. "Nirvana, the sex pistols, the food fighters, nine inch nails, REM smashing pumpkins, the killers, Scott Wyland, Coldplay. They all have bits of Bowie DNA in their sound and vision."

xref.title: Influence on Alt-Rock Icons
xref.body: Despite his humble beginnings with The Shades, Lou Reed later became a foundational influence on many significant artists in the alt-rock scene. His work inspired figures such as David Bowie, Iggy Pop, R.E.M., and The Killers. "he would later influence Bowie and Iggy and R.E.M. and the killers and so many of the other movers and shakers of the alt-rock scene in the decades ahead."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Book of World Records Version 1.0 - Part 2

xref.title: Influence on Alternative Generation
xref.body: The Pixies are recognized as part of the alternative generation profoundly influenced by David Bowie. Bowie's "shape-shifting style" and introduction of "more theater, fantasy, and imagination" into rock and roll culture provided foundational inspiration for bands like the Pixies. "His effect on the alternative generation from the Pixies to Nirvana to Nine-inch Nails to Arcade Fire."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence on Bowie and Punk
xref.body: Lou Reed was a new friend who inspired David Bowie's glam rock experimentation. His past membership in The Velvet Underground, coupled with his friendship with Bowie, also made Bowie "cool" in the eyes of the early British punks. "Inspired by Bowlin, his crazy new friend Iggy Pop, Lou Reed, another new friend."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence on British Punks
xref.body: Similar to David Bowie, Roxy Music garnered the attention of young people who would later become British punks, partly because their artifice and experimental sound, especially the synthesizer-heavy Side Two, were disliked by mainstream critics. "Like Bowie, Roxy Music attracted the attention of kids who would soon become Britain's punks. They especially liked that the critics weren't crazy about Roxy Music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

xref.title: Influence on David Bowie
xref.body: David Bowie was a fan of The Velvet Underground, contributing to his inspirations for the Ziggy Stardust character. "He was a fan of both Reed's band, the Velvet Underground."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

xref.title: Influence on David Bowie
xref.body: David Bowie was deeply interested in Kraftwerk and the rising sound of synthesizers in Germany, which significantly influenced his musical evolution towards electronic methods of production and his move to Berlin. "He was deeply interested in what was happening in Germany with groups such as Kraftwerk, Ken, New, and the rising sound of synthesizers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence on David Bowie's Berlin Period
xref.body: David Bowie discovered and was hugely enamored with the electronic sounds of Kraftwerk during his time in Berlin. Their music, along with that of Neu!, significantly influenced Bowie's shift towards electronic methods of music production and contributed to the sound of his Berlin trilogy albums. "Bowie was hugely enamored with German electronic music, specifically craft work."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence on Future Artists
xref.body: Noel Coward continued to make music for West End and Broadway in the mid-1960s, which introduced his work to a new generation, including a young David Bowie, the future founder of Roxy Music, and Alice Cooper. "And this is how a new generation learned about him, and that included a young David Bowie, and the young man who would later form Roxy Music, and Alice Cooper."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

xref.title: Influence on Industrial Music
xref.body: David Bowie was a very important figure for fans of industrial music, especially those who admired Nine Inch Nails. His experimental and electronic work from the Berlin period laid groundwork that resonated deeply within the industrial genre. "And if you loved industrial music, Bowie was very important to you, especially if you were a fan of 9-inch nails."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence on New Romanticism
xref.body: The band's style provided inspiration for the New Romanticism movement, alongside David Bowie and Brian Eno. "Taking cues from David Bowie and Roxy Music and Brian Eno."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Roots of New Wave through Techno-Pop

xref.title: Influence on New Romanticism
xref.body: His artistic contributions served as an influence for the New Romanticism movement, alongside David Bowie and Roxy Music. "Taking cues from David Bowie and Roxy Music and Brian Eno."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Roots of New Wave through Techno-Pop

xref.title: Influence on Punk Rock
xref.body: Despite remaining fringe figures, the first three albums by The Stooges, particularly through David Bowie's influence and acceptance of their unconventional style, became fundamental templates for the development of punk rock. Their raw energy and disregard for mainstream rock conventions inspired a new generation of musicians. "And this is how the first three Stooges albums became some of the most important templates for what would be eventually called punk rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influenced Major Artists
xref.body: The Velvet Underground is credited with awakening and influencing a wide array of prominent artists and bands, including David Bowie, Roxy Music, The Doors, Patti Smith, Iggy Pop and the Stooges, U2, Joy Division, The Pixies, The Sex Pistols, Talking Heads, The Cure, Kraftwerk, R.E.M., Simple Minds, The Strokes, and The Psychedelic Furs, whose name derived from a Velvet Underground song. "Here is a list of just some of the few who claimed to have been awakened by the velvet underground and then incorporated some of whatever they were doing into their music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Peaked Too Soon - Bands That Were Ahead of Their Time

xref.title: Influenced by Bowie and Kraftwerk
xref.body: Miller was influenced by the electronic music of David Bowie and Kraftwerk, combining the concept of stylish, futuristic, machine-generated music with punk rock's DIY aesthetic. "Like a number of young British musicians, Miller had been exposed to craft work and the electronic musings of David Bowie."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influenced by Bowie's Shape-Shifting Style
xref.body: Madonna is among the artists who have imitated David Bowie's shape-shifting style, demonstrating his profound and widespread influence on performers who continuously reinvent their image and artistry. "Madonna, Lady Gaga, Prince. The list is endless."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influenced by Bowie's Shape-Shifting Style
xref.body: Lady Gaga is among the artists who have imitated David Bowie's shape-shifting style, showcasing his enduring legacy as a trendsetter and cultural mover and shaker who inspired other artists to explore theatricality and image transformation. "Madonna, Lady Gaga, Prince. The list is endless."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influenced by David Bowie
xref.body: Prince is listed among the many artists whose music and artistry have been influenced by David Bowie, demonstrating the wide and lasting impact Bowie had across various genres and styles. "Madonna, Lady Gaga, Prince. The list is endless."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influential Robotic Sound
xref.body: Kraftwerk's music from the late 1970s, exemplified by "The Model," was characterized by a robotic, cold, deliberately artificial, emotionally sterile, and intense vibe. This sound was a significant part of early Technopop and greatly intrigued and influenced artists like David Bowie. "And note the vibe of that song. Much of early technopop was robotic, cold, deliberately artificial, emotionally sterile, and just generally a little intense. That description can also be applied to craft work, the normal and some of Bowie's electronic experiments."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Initial Band Name
xref.body: The band that would become Joy Division initially went by the name "Warsaw" after Ian Curtis rejected "Stiff Kittens." This name was inspired by David Bowie's song "Warzawe" from his "Low" album. "Everyone soon settled on Warsaw. That sounded different."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

xref.title: Inspiration for "TVC-15"
xref.body: Iggy Pop was involved in a dream or drug-induced hallucination with David Bowie that served as the inspiration for Bowie's song "TVC-15." "It was inspired by a dream, more likely a drug-induced hallucination with his friend, Ike Pop, where an unidentified girlfriend was eaten by a holographic television, model number, TVC-15."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Inspiration for Dark Music
xref.body: Joy Division's dark music attracted punk refugees looking for gloomy sounds during a difficult time in England. "That would include David Bowie and joint-evision, the first version of Ultravox, and an Irish performance art group called The Virgin Proons."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Inspiration for David Bowie's "Stardust"
xref.body: When David Bowie signed with Mercury Records in 1970, he received a stack of 7-inch singles, which included Norm O'Dam's "Paralyzed." Bowie, who was "no stranger to chemicals in those days," became obsessed with the record and the artist, eventually appropriating the "Stardust" part of "The Legendary Stardust Cowboy" for his iconic Ziggy Stardust character. "Bowie appropriated the Stardust part of the legendary Stardust cowboy for his new creation."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Inspiration for Tin Machine
xref.body: Jimi Hendrix was cited as an inspiration for David Bowie's band Tin Machine. Bowie's idea was to form a four-piece rock band with himself purely as the lead singer, drawing on the raw energy and format of such influential artists. "Inspiration was taken from Jimmy Hendrix, Cream and the Pixies."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Inspiration for Tin Machine
xref.body: Cream was cited as an inspiration for David Bowie's band Tin Machine. Bowie aimed to create a four-piece rock band with himself solely as the lead singer, harkening back to the dynamic and influential styles of bands like Cream. "Inspiration was taken from Jimmy Hendrix, Cream and the Pixies."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Inspiration for Tin Machine
xref.body: The Pixies were cited as an inspiration for David Bowie's band Tin Machine. Bowie's vision for Tin Machine was a four-piece rock band where he would primarily serve as the lead singer, drawing inspiration from the raw, impactful sound of bands like the Pixies. "Inspiration was taken from Jimmy Hendrix, Cream and the Pixies."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Inspiration for Ziggy Stardust
xref.body: Iggy Pop, a friend of David Bowie, was one of the two people who inspired the name for Bowie's alien rock star character, Ziggy, in *The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust and The Spiders from Mars*. "And that name was inspired by two people, Bowie's new friend Iggy Pop, and a Texas proto-psychobilly singer named Norman O'Dan, who went by the handle of the legendary Stardust Cowboy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Inspiration for Ziggy Stardust
xref.body: Norman O'Dan, a Texas proto-psychobilly singer also known as The Legendary Stardust Cowboy, was a big fan of space travel and admired by David Bowie. He was one of the two people who inspired the name for Bowie's alien rock star character, Ziggy, in *The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust and The Spiders from Mars*. "And that name was inspired by two people, Bowie's new friend Iggy Pop, and a Texas proto-psychobilly singer named Norman O'Dan, who went by the handle of the legendary Stardust Cowboy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Jimmy Page's Occult Involvement (Mid-1970s)
xref.body: Led Zeppelin guitarist Jimmy Page was known for his deep involvement in the occult. This fascination reportedly influenced David Bowie, who believed that his association with Page had put his soul in danger, contributing to Bowie's drug-induced paranoia about witches. "Page was deep into the occult."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Joey Ramone's Early Glam Phase
xref.body: Around his 21st birthday, Joey became deeply immersed in glam culture, idolizing David Bowie and Alice Cooper. He would dress in satin jumpsuits adorned with rhinestones and wear knee-high platform boots, which exaggerated his height to six feet eight inches. "He also became a big fan of Alice Cooper. His first real band was called Sniper."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Key Contributor to Bowie's Berlin Trilogy
xref.body: Brian Eno made significant contributions to David Bowie's albums "Low" (especially Side 2) and "Lodger" during the Berlin trilogy period. While he did not produce "Lodger" (Tony Visconti did), he played an essential role in helping Bowie explore his musical ideas. "Brian Eno was there to make some important contributions."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Laying Punk Rock Foundations – Post-Drumming Career
xref.body: Iggy Pop eventually moved from behind the drum kit to start writing songs, leading to the formation of The Stooges. His career further evolved with involvement from David Bowie and significant personal experiences, which collectively laid the foundations for modern punk rock. "He started writing songs moved on to the stooges got involved with David Bowie took a lot of LSD and pretty much laid the foundations for modern punk rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Long-term Collaborator with David Bowie
xref.body: Mike Garson played with David Bowie for many years, showcasing his distinctive piano talents. He is identified as David Bowie's favorite piano player, highlighting his significant role in Bowie's musical output. "Mike Garcin, who played with Boie for years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: MTV Unplugged Performance
xref.body: Stone Temple Pilots performed for MTV Unplugged, with their episode broadcast on November 17, 1993. Notably, this performance took place in the same studio where Nirvana recorded their famous MTV Unplugged performance, just one day prior to Nirvana's session. Both bands chose to cover semi-obscure songs by David Bowie as part of their sets. "On Temple Pilots, performing for MTV with an unplugged episode broadcast on November 17, 1993."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: MTV Unplugged Performance
xref.body: Nirvana recorded their famous MTV Unplugged performance in the same studio as Stone Temple Pilots, one day after STP's broadcast on November 17, 1993. Like STP, Nirvana also chose to cover semi-obscure songs by David Bowie during their set. "that by the way was one day before Nirvana set up in the same studio to record their famous unplugged performance."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Managerial Support for Bowie's Image (Late 1970s)
xref.body: Tony DeFries became David Bowie's manager in the late 1970s and was highly supportive of Bowie's innovative artistic endeavors, including his experimental approach to rock music and his decision to wear a dress in public. "And he was only too happy to help Bowie search for a new approach to rock music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 1

xref.title: Marriage to May Pang
xref.body: Tony Visconti, a producer for David Bowie, married May Pang, who was John Lennon's assistant during his "lost weekend" period from Yoko Ono. "Not only did he and Bowie get along famously but so did Lennon's assistant May Pang and Bowie producer Tony Viscante and they actually ended up getting married."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Marriage to Suci
xref.body: Iggy Pop met and married a Japanese woman named Suci during a period of renewed stability in his life, following a career boost from David Bowie's recording of "China Girl." "Iggy then met and married a Japanese woman named Suci."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About Iggy Pop

xref.title: Mental Hospital Stay
xref.body: Iggy Pop checked himself into a mental hospital, which was described as "one of the wisest things he'd ever done." His "only visitor" during this time was David Bowie, who brought him drugs. "Now it was true that Iggy Pop had checked himself into a mental hospital, which was one of the wisest things he'd ever done, but he had already made his point."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Move to Berlin with Bowie
xref.body: Iggy Pop packed up and left Los Angeles with David Bowie to move to Berlin, Germany, during the height of the Cold War. This move allowed them to immerse themselves in Berlin's unique artistic and bohemian culture. "He and Iggy Pop packed up and left for Berlin."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Musical Influences and Punk Attitude
xref.body: Oasis's debut album combined new and familiar sounds, incorporating elements of The Beatles, David Bowie, T-Rex, The Jam, The Stones, and The Stone Roses. Their songs were delivered with an intense, almost punk attitude, creating guitar pop as loud as the Sex Pistols but with more groove and melody. "There were bits of Beatles, it's a Bowie and T-Rex and the Jam and the Stones and the Stone Roses in there."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

xref.title: Musical Mentorship and Contribution
xref.body: Ronnie Ross played the saxophone part on Lou Reed's "Walk on the Wild Side." He also had a significant connection to David Bowie, having taught Bowie how to play the saxophone back in the 1950s. "The saxophone bit at the end was played by Ronnie Ross, the guy who taught Bowie how to play sax when he was a kid back in the 1950s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Name "Warsaw" Inspiration
xref.body: After rejecting "Stiff Kittens," the band settled on "Warsaw," inspired by the song "Warzawe" from David Bowie's "Low" album, reflecting Ian Curtis's admiration for Bowie. "Besides, they were inspired by a song called Warzawe on David Bowie's low album."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

xref.title: New Romantic Descendant
xref.body: Duran Duran is identified as a band that emerged from the New Romantic movement, directly influenced by the legacy of glam rock, particularly David Bowie and Roxy Music. "bands like Durand, Iran."

xref.title: New York Artsy Scummy Solo Persona
xref.body: Lou Reed's "New York Artsy Scummy solo persona" and his work with The Velvet Underground were admired by David Bowie and served as an influence for the Ziggy Stardust character. "Reed's New York Artsy Scummy solo persona."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

xref.title: New York Underground and David Bowie Collaboration
xref.body: Nomi became a prominent figure in the New York Underground scene, gaining recognition from artists such as Keith Haring and Jean-Michel Basquiat. David Bowie, upon hearing about Nomi, rushed to see one of his live shows. This led to Nomi's appearance with Bowie on Saturday Night Live on December 15, 1979, where Nomi sang backup on three songs. "He became a fixture in the New York Underground scene and was embraced by artists such as Keith Haring and Johnny Shell Basquit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Notable Clients and Recordings
xref.body: Many famous artists recorded and performed at the Château. The Grateful Dead recorded there and played a show on its grounds. Elton John named his 1972 album after the place (the first of three he recorded there). Pink Floyd, T. Rex, David Bowie, Fleetwood Mac, and Iggy Pop (who recorded his 1977 album *The Idiot* with Bowie) also utilized the studio. "The Grateful Dad not only recorded there, but played a show on its grounds."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Number One Records in 2010s
xref.body: Fall Out Boy was among the artists, including Blink-182, Green Day, Coldplay, Jack White, Red Hot Chili Peppers, Slipknot, Queens of the Stone Age, Pearl Jam, Foo Fighters, U2, Linkin Park, Evanescence, and David Bowie, who achieved number one records during the 2010s. This demonstrated the continued success of rock acts in an era where hip hop was a dominant cultural force. "Link wanted a two Green Day Coldplay Jack White, Red Hotch-Lie Pepper, Slipp-Nont, Queens of the Stone Age, Pearl Jam, Foo Fighters, U2, Link and Park Follow Boy, Evan Essence, Queens of the Stone Age, and Bowie all had number one records over the course of the decade."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 4: The Revivals

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 4: The Revivals

xref.title: Origin as Snow White Tan
xref.body: Chester Bennington's side project was initially known as "Snow White Tan," a name that was recognized as a possible reference to David Bowie and his Ziggy Stardust persona, before eventually changing to Dead by Sunrise. "his own side project, which was first called Snow White Tan. Notice the reference to Bowie and Zee Stardust, and then Dead by Sunrise."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Origin from Blitz Kids Movement
xref.body: Visage was fronted by Steve Strange, who gained recognition as one of the Blitz kids featured in David Bowie's "Ashes to Ashes" video. The band's emergence reflects its roots in the Blitz kids' subculture and the broader New Romantic movement. "Steve Strange, one of the people in that video, would later front of band called Visage, which did okay."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Outrageous Behavior
xref.body: Iggy Pop was known for his "outrageous behavior" and "extreme things" performed with his band The Stooges in America, which directly influenced David Bowie's creation of the Ziggy Stardust character. "Iggy Pop, who was doing all kinds of extreme things in America with his band, The Stooges."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

xref.title: Pioneers of Over-the-Top Glam Makeup
xref.body: The New York Dolls were notable for their adoption of over-the-top glam makeup styles during the early 1970s, contributing to the flamboyant visual aesthetic of the era. "Styles run from the over-the-top glam of David Bowie and the New York Dolls in the early 1970s..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Possible Inspiration for Bowie's "Heroes"
xref.body: Tony Visconti and his girlfriend, Antonia Maass, were possibly the young couple David Bowie saw kissing by the Berlin Wall from the studio window, an event that allegedly inspired the song "Heroes." "This was possibly producer Tony Visconti and his girlfriend, Antonio Moss."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Post-Bowie Career Slump and Resurgence
xref.body: After a strong start with Bowie, Iggy Pop's solo career sagged by 1982, leaving him without a record contract and forced to tour to survive. However, David Bowie again intervened with his recording of "China Girl," which provided a financial turnaround, leading to the phrase, "This guy's got more lives in a cat, doesn't he?" "Fortunately though, his old pal David Bowie came through right about then with his recording of China Girl, and things turned around again."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About Iggy Pop

xref.title: Post-Bowie Death Tribute
xref.body: After David Bowie's death in 2016, Kanye West was among the first artists to post a tribute to him on Twitter, which some conspiracy theorists see as further evidence of a connection between the two. Stories also circulated that Kanye was planning a Bowie tribute album. "When Bowie died in 2016, Kanye was among the first to post a tribute to him on Twitter."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Praise for Arcade Fire
xref.body: Chris Martin, among other "big name stars," has "lavished praise" on Arcade Fire's work. "Big name stars, all the way up to Chris Martin and you two and David Bowie have lavished praise on them."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Who the Hell is Arcade Fire? Part 2

xref.title: Probable Bisexuality
xref.body: Similar to David Bowie, Lou Reed was likely bisexual. His public persona and lyrical content often suggested a fluid sexuality, which was reinforced by his marriage to a woman in 1973 combined with the explicit themes in his music. "Probably bisexual, just like Bowie, and Little Richard admitted to being something after all his early success."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Early Days of LGBTQ Rock

xref.title: Produced by Brian Eno
xref.body: Brian Eno produced records for the band Talking Heads. "He's produced records for David Bowie, you two, the Talking Hits and Coldplay"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Producer for David Bowie's Lodger
xref.body: Tony Visconti served as the producer for David Bowie's album "Lodger." "That was still Tony Visconti's job."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Producer for Renowned Artists
xref.body: Eno has a distinguished career as a record producer, having worked on albums for iconic artists such as David Bowie, U2, Talking Heads, and Coldplay. "He's produced records for David Bowie, you two, the Talking Hits and Coldplay"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Pushing for Better Sound
xref.body: Supertramp was among the bands, including David Bowie and Yes, who actively pushed sound companies to improve their live audio. They considered "getting concert sound right was very, very important," thereby influencing the advancement of concert sound systems and techniques. "But to performers like David Bowie and Yes and Super Tramp, getting concert sound right was very, very important, so they pushed sound companies to get better."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Recording "Life on Mars" Piano Part
xref.body: While recording David Bowie's "Life on Mars," Rick Wakeman played the 100-year-old Bechstein piano, and it's noted that microphones might have been set up in the men's bathroom to capture its special natural reverb. "It's also quite possible that the microphones were arranged in the nearby men's bathroom, because there was something special about the natural reverb in there that just made a recording sound so special."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
